Add a market-map diagram (ideally interactive: drag a brand onto price/quality axes) and an adding-value bar (input cost vs selling price); attach quiz[6]/[7] and a practice item to block 5 so the section does not end unchecked.

Fill spec gaps inside Learn Mode: market size/share/growth with a worked calculation, brands and brand loyalty, ICT in market research (websites, social media analytics, databases), online retailing as a driver of dynamic markets; shrink the sampling block to a single 'sample size and bias' subsection.

Clean the quiz bank: delete duplicates (10, 12, 15, one of 4/18), fix ambiguous items 3 (add 'random selection within each group'), 16 (add a numeric cue), 17 (reclassify or teach ICT-sourced data first), 7 (reword correct option as a difference, not a price rise), and remove absolute-word distractors in 20/22/24.

q3: Quota sampling ALSO divides the population into subgroups and fills proportionate targets from each; the only real discriminator (random vs non-random selection within groups) is absent from the stem. Options B (quota) and C (stratified) are both defensible. Explanation's 'without the same systematic approach' does not resolve it.

q16: Stem contains no numerical data; surveys can be qualitative (open questions). 'Primary qualitative research' (option B) is equally defensible. Needs a numeric cue (e.g. '68% of 2,000 respondents').

p0: 'Define the term niche market (4 marks)' — IAL Business definitions are 2-mark 'What is meant by...' items. The guidance pads to 4 by crediting an example and 'premium pricing', neither of which is part of a definition. Teaches the wrong exam shape.
p1: 'Explain two benefits ... (6 marks)' — IAL uses 'Explain one ...' for 4 marks (K1/A1/An2 chain). There is no 6-mark explain-two format on WBS11. Guidance also has no application requirement.

p4: 'Outline two features of a dynamic market (4 marks)' — 'Outline' is not an IAL Business command word (it is GCSE/other boards). Should be 'Explain one feature...' (4) or 'What is meant by a dynamic market?' (2).
Zero recall widgets (0 reorder, 0 fillin) across 15 subsections — the spaced/immediate retrieval mechanic that defines Learn Mode never fires; the section is read-only plus one MCQ per block.

Zero diagrams. Market mapping is the canonical diagram of this topic and its own examMatters says 'questions often provide a diagram' — yet no market map is shown. Adding value (input cost vs price bar) and mass/niche positioning are also natural diagrams.

practiceIndices are attached to the wrong blocks: block 1 'Competition, Risk and Uncertainty' → practice[0] (define niche market); block 2 'Market Research Methods' → practice[1] (benefits of niche market); block 4 'Market Positioning and Orientation' → practice[2] (market research in a dynamic market). Block 0, where all the niche/mass/dynamic content lives, gets no practice. Correct mapping: practice 0,1,3,4 → block 0; practice 2 → block 2.

Block 5 'Segmentation and Competitive Advantage' has no quizIndices and no practiceIndices even though quiz[6] (segmentation bases) and quiz[7] (adding value) exist. The section ends on three subsections with no check for understanding.
Only 5 of 25 MCQs are used inline (one per block); 20 sit unused except via random PreTest/PostTest draws.

Spec ordering is scrambled: product vs market orientation (spec 1.1.2a, market research) is placed in the 'Positioning' block; segmentation (1.1.2e) is placed with competitive advantage/adding value (1.1.3). A student following the spec cannot map blocks to spec bullets.

Weighting: a full block (2 subsections + 1 inline MCQ) on sampling methods that are not on the IAL spec, while spec bullets market size/share, brands, ICT in research and online retailing are absent from Learn Mode (they exist only in the Notes tab as 'Market Size, Share & Growth' and 'Branding').

2-per-step pairing: block 0 pairs (mass, niche) then leaves 'dynamic-markets' alone; block 2 leaves 'qualitative-vs-quantitative' alone; block 5 leaves 'adding-value' alone as the final step with no quiz — a weak finale. Pairings themselves are coherent.
Takeaways match their blocks well (good). Block 4 has 4 takeaways vs 3 elsewhere; fine.

Some FLOW chains are filler rather than causal: 'Research customer needs → Design product to match → Launch with confidence'; 'Identify existing data sources → Analyse data for your purpose' (2-step). The dynamic-markets flow is non-causal (see accuracy).
Misconceptions are genuine student errors (risk=uncertainty, segmentation=targeting, adding value=raising price, gap=opportunity, bigger sample=better) — this is a strength, not filler.

Difficulty ramp is flat: every subsection follows the identical template; there is no build from definition → application → evaluation within the section, so the 20-mark evaluate question at the end has no scaffolding step before it.
1.1.1a Market size and market share — definitions and the share/growth calculations are not in Learn Mode content (only in the Notes tab).
1.1.1a Brands — branding as a characteristic of mass markets is mentioned in one clause; no teaching of brand, brand loyalty, or brands as barriers to entry (Notes tab has it, Learn Mode does not).

1.1.1b Dynamic markets: online retailing; innovation and market growth; adapting to change — only one passing sentence ('Online retailing, streaming services and electric vehicles are all examples'); no treatment of how online retailing changes markets or of innovation driving market growth.
1.1.2b Market research used to quantify likely demand — not covered; research is framed only as identifying needs and gaining insight.

1.1.2c Limitations of market research (as a topic) — only implied via sampling bias; no explicit treatment of cost, time, consumers not doing what they say, research becoming outdated (the practice[2] guidance expects these).
1.1.2d Use of ICT to support market research: websites, social networking, databases — not taught at all, yet quiz[17] tests it.
1.1.3a Market mapping — taught in text but the spec skill (interpreting/drawing a map) is untested because there is no diagram.

Add the three referenced diagrams (demand shift D1->D2, supply shift S1->S2, equilibrium with surplus/shortage and Pe/Qe) so InlineDiagram actually renders; add a TR/elasticity diagram for ped-and-revenue. This is the spec's own bullet (1.2.3b) and currently absent.

Re-wire quizIndices/practiceIndices so each block's inline MCQ and practice question are on-topic (e.g. block1->Q2, block2->Q4, block3->Q9, block4->Q6), and replace the two off-topic practice questions (market positioning 20-marker, market share Outline) with on-spec IAL-tariffed items: Calculate PED/YED (4), Draw a diagram to show… (4), Explain (4), Analyse (6), Assess a pricing decision given PED (10/12), Evaluate with a short case (20) — with levels-based guidance.
Fix or delete quiz Q18 (revenue is unchanged at $20,000; explanation contains an unfinished authoring note) and drop Q14 (price elasticity of supply is not in the IAL Business spec).

Correct the false/backwards real examples: UK strawberries (illustrates a seasonal supply shift, not the law of supply), UK tobacco duty (receipts have fallen since 2021-22; also tax revenue != firm TR), Sony PS5 2024 (Sony raised, not cut, prices); and rebalance the UK-heavy example set toward the app's Asian/Middle-East cohorts.

Remove first-letter hints from all six fillins (or make them optional after a wrong attempt) and replace the two non-causal reorders (PED goods ranking; recession/YED parallel outcomes) with classify/sort or numeric fillin exercises; move the extras chains/evaluation (all 1.1 market research content) to meeting-customer-needs and write on-topic ones (e.g. 'Cost-push shock -> supply shifts left -> price up, quantity down -> firms with inelastic demand pass costs on').

Supply and Factors Affecting Supply > what-is-supply > realExample (UK strawberry farmers): Backwards and teaches the wrong concept. UK strawberry retail prices are LOWEST in summer because that is peak season; farmers supply more in summer because of growing conditions (seasonality = a supply SHIFT), not because 'retail prices are highest'. Presented as 'the law of supply in action' (movement along the curve), it is a textbook example of the opposite. Also UK-centric for an international cohort.
content.evidence: audit/snapshots/2026-09-11-post-packet-0__business__the-market.json content>what-is-supply>realExample.text now reads 'Ride-hailing drivers ... movement along the supply curve'; law-of-supply/shift confusion removed

content.text: Price Elasticity of Demand (PED) > ped-and-revenue > realExample (UK government tobacco taxation): Claims 'total tax revenue increases each year'. HMRC tobacco duty receipts peaked around 2021-22 (~£10.3bn) and have fallen since (~£8.8bn 2023-24, lower again 2024-25). Also conflates government tax revenue with a firm's total revenue (TR = P x Q), which is the concept being taught; the addictive-good framing is Economics 2.x/market failure territory.

Demand and Factors Affecting Demand > what-is-demand > realExample (Sony PS5): 'Sony cut the price of the PS5 in several markets to boost sales in 2024. As the price dropped, quantity demanded rose sharply.' Sony's headline 2024 move was a ~19% price RISE in Japan (Sept 2024), followed by rises in Europe/UK/Australia (Apr 2025) and the US (Aug 2025); 2024 saw only short promotional discounts, and PS5 shipments fell year-on-year in FY2024. The example as written is not true and will confuse students who read the news.

q18: Internally inconsistent and the explanation is unfinished. Revenue is exactly unchanged (500x$40 = $20,000; 400x$50 = $20,000), yet the keyed answer [0] says 'demand is inelastic so revenue rises'. The explanation literally contains 'Revenue rises from $20,000 to $20,000... actually revenue = ... However…' — a visible authoring note. A numerate student who checks the arithmetic will (correctly) reject the keyed answer.
content.evidence: audit/snapshots/2026-09-11-post-packet-0__business__the-market.json quiz[18]: membership now 500->450, explanation reworked to PED=-0.4 and revenue 20000->22500, no unfinished authoring note

content.text: q14: Price elasticity of SUPPLY is not in the IAL Business specification (only PED and YED in 1.2.4/1.2.5) and is not taught anywhere in this section. Out-of-spec question; explanation does not address the distractors.

p3: OFF-TOPIC: 'Evaluate the factors that determine the market positioning of a new product… (20 marks)' is 1.1.3 Market positioning, not The Market. Also a 20-mark IAL Business Evaluate is always case-study based with stimulus data; none is provided. The guidance is points-based ('3 marks' per factor, '2 marks' for intro) whereas IAL 20-markers are levels-marked (Knowledge/Application/Analysis/Evaluation, Levels 1-4) — the model answer teaches the wrong marking model.
content.evidence: audit/snapshots/2026-09-11-post-packet-0__business__the-market.json practice[3] ('market positioning' 20-marker) hidden:true, no longer served by PracticeQuestionsTab (isPracticeVisible filters .hidden)

content.text: p4: OFF-TOPIC: 'Outline two ways a business could increase its market share (4 marks)' is 1.1.1 The market (market share), not demand/supply/elasticity. 'Outline' is not an IAL Business command word (Define/State/Explain/Calculate/Draw/Analyse/Assess/Discuss/Evaluate).

p2: 'Analyse … (10 marks)': in IAL Business, Analyse is a 6-mark command; 10/12 marks are 'Assess'. The guidance awards 2 marks for 'Judgement on how useful YED is' — evaluation is not credited under Analyse. Points-style '(2 marks)' allocations again misrepresent levels marking. Content-wise the question is on-topic and good.

p0: 'Define PED (4 marks)': Define is a 2-mark command in WBS11; a 4-mark tariff does not exist. The guidance pads to 4 by adding elastic/inelastic interpretation, which is not part of a definition. Also wired as the inline practice for the Market Equilibrium block (practiceIndices [0]), so students meet a PED definition question before PED is taught.

ZERO DIAGRAMS: blocks 0-2 carry diagramRef 'demand-curve', 'supply-curve', 'equilibrium-diagram' but diagrams[] is empty (meta.diagrams: 0), so InlineDiagram never renders. The prose repeatedly says 'on a diagram…', examMatters demand D1/D2, S1/S2, Pe/Qe labelling, and spec 1.2.3(b) is literally 'supply and demand diagrams'. Highest-impact gap in the section; PED/YED blocks have no diagramRef at all (a TR-under-elastic/inelastic diagram would help ped-and-revenue).

INLINE QUIZ WIRING OFF BY ONE: quizIndices are [0],[1],[2],[3],[4] but quiz[1] is PED/revenue (shown at end of Supply block), quiz[2] is a supply shift (shown at end of Equilibrium block), quiz[3] is YED (shown at end of PED block), quiz[4] is equilibrium (shown at end of YED block). Only block 0 gets an on-topic inline MCQ. Suggested map: block0->Q0 or Q12; block1->Q2 or Q17; block2->Q4 or Q11 or Q19; block3->Q7/Q9/Q15; block4->Q6/Q16/Q23.

INLINE PRACTICE WIRING: practiceIndices [0] (Define PED) on the Equilibrium block, [1] (demand-shift Explain) on the PED block. Both are one block out of place; blocks 0, 1 and 4 get no practice at all despite on-topic candidates existing.

EXTRAS ARE THE WRONG SECTION: all 4 chains (market research, segmentation, market size/growth/share, market mapping) and all 3 evaluation points (primary research cost, segmentation oversimplifies, data becomes outdated) belong to 1.1 Meeting Customer Needs. Nothing in extras touches demand, supply, equilibrium, PED or YED. Flashcard 22/25 ('Trace how high competition in a market affects…') and duplicated flashcards 20-22 = 23-25 show the same copy-paste origin.

2-per-step pairing: block 3 (PED) has 3 subsections, so calculating-ped + factors-affecting-ped form one step and ped-and-revenue sits alone on the block's last step with the inline quiz (currently the YED Q3), practice, ExplainItBack and takeaway — the heaviest concept in the section is the most cluttered step. Consider splitting PED into two blocks (calc+factors / revenue) each with its own quiz.

Recall placement: factors-shifting-demand's reorder ends with 'Equilibrium price and quantity both increase', which is not taught until block 3 (Market Equilibrium). Served as the 'spaced' recall at the top of the Supply step, it references a concept the student has not yet met.

Difficulty ramp is sensible (definition -> shift factors -> equilibrium -> PED -> YED) and matches the spec order. Takeaways match their blocks accurately. Misconceptions are real ones (movement vs shift, equilibrium != fair, PED sign, price cut != more revenue, inferior != low quality) — not filler. Only factors-affecting-ped's misconception ('students list factors without applying') is a study-skills note rather than a conceptual misconception.
Fillin hint design is systemic: all 16 hints across 6 fillins are first-letters-plus-length ('mov_____'), making every fillin a copy exercise. This is a component-level pattern, not a per-item slip.

Exam-tips in common_mistakes ('extension/contraction in demand') use terminology the main content never introduces (content only says 'movement along'); flashcard 2 also uses extension/contraction. Align: introduce extension/contraction once in what-is-demand.

Regional skew: 7 of 11 real examples are UK-based (Sony aside: Oatly ok, UK strawberries, UK housing, UK energy/British Gas, UK tobacco tax, Aldi/Lidl UK, Ryanair). Target students are in HK/SG/MY/PK/LK/ME; at least half should be regional or global.

1.2.1 Demand — factors leading to a change in demand: 'advertising and branding' (only alluded to inside 'tastes'), 'external shocks' and 'seasonality' are not taught for demand (seasonality appears nowhere; it is arguably the mis-described strawberry example).

Inventory Management > just-in-time > realExample: Claims Toyota 'had to halt production at 14 factories because its JIT system had no buffer stock of chips' in the 2021 semiconductor shortage. This inverts the well-documented story: after the 2011 Fukushima earthquake Toyota deliberately built a business-continuity plan holding 2-6 months of chip stock, and in early 2021 it was widely reported as the carmaker LEAST affected by the chip shortage precisely because it broke from pure JIT for semiconductors. The August/September 2021 cuts at 14 plants were driven mainly by COVID outbreaks at parts suppliers in Malaysia/Vietnam. A student who repeats this line to an examiner who knows the case loses credibility.

Practice questions 2, 3, 4 are never surfaced inline (practiceIndices only on blocks 1 and 2); Block 0 and Block 3 have no InlinePractice.
Block 2 takeaway[0] ('JIT eliminates stock-holding costs') contradicts the block's own misconception ('minimise, not eliminate'). Block 3 takeaways are fine; Block 0 and 1 takeaways match content.

Misconceptions: productivity vs production, JIT = zero stock, lean = JIT, 100% utilisation is ideal, and 'just cut prices' are genuine student errors. 'TQM guarantees zero defects', 'QC is a bad method businesses should never use' and 'kaizen is a one-off project' are weaker/filler - few students actually write these; better real ones: 'capacity utilisation above 100% is possible', 'QA means no inspection at all', 'higher productivity means workers work harder'.

Difficulty ramp is acceptable (definitions and calculation early, evaluative content later), but the section never moves from 'describe' to 'apply to context': no worked capacity-utilisation or productivity calculation with a twist (e.g. capacity changes after rationalisation), which is where IAL marks are lost.
2.4.3a Interpretation of stock control diagrams: buffer stock, re-order level, re-order quantity, lead time, maximum stock level - entirely absent (no diagram, no text).
2.4.3b/c Buffer stocks and implications of poor stock control (stock-outs, obsolescence, cash tied up, storage costs) - only implicit inside the JIT subsection; never taught as its own idea.
2.4.1c Efficiency defined as production at minimum average cost, and factors influencing efficiency - not taught; 'efficiency' is used loosely as a synonym for productivity.
2.4.1a Cell production as a method of production - mentioned in one clause under lean and used as a quiz distractor, but not taught (the section says 'job, batch or flow' only).

2.4.1b Factors influencing productivity (training, technology, motivation, working practices) and the productivity-competitiveness link - present but thin; no worked calculation of output per worker per period with a comparison over time.
2.4.4c Quality circles as a distinct technique - only aliased inside kaizen.
2.4.3e/f Waste minimisation and competitive advantage from lean production - competitive advantage is in extras chains only, not in Learn Mode content.
2.4.2b Implications of OVER-utilisation - covered in one paragraph and practice Q4, adequate.
Spec numbering: content sits under 2.3.4 but IAL Resource management is 2.4 (unsure of app's numbering convention; verify).

Add the missing half of the topic: a block on 1.5.6 Moving from entrepreneur to leader (difficulties + how to overcome) and a block on 1.5.4 Forms of business (sole trader/partnership/Ltd/franchise/social enterprise/lifestyle/online/PLC + liability); then the leadership practice question and flashcards actually have content behind them.

Replace the 12 recall widgets: drop letter-leaking hints; convert the five fillins to scenario->concept matches or a numeric opportunity-cost calc; convert the non-financial 'rank by popularity' and the objectives/conflicts/trade-offs reorders to classify/match tasks; keep only the intrapreneurship reorder.

q2: Fine as a question, but it is assigned as Block 2's (Business Objectives) inline quiz — it belongs to Block 0 (Barriers). quizIndices are sequential 0,1,2,3 rather than topic-matched.

p2: 'Assess the importance of leadership style... (10 marks)': leadership styles (autocratic, democratic, paternalistic, laissez-faire) are not taught anywhere in this section's content — they are 1.4.5 Managing People content — and 1.5.6 'moving from entrepreneur to leader', which would justify it, is absent. Title/coverage mismatch: section is 'Entrepreneurs and Leaders' (IAL 1.5) but has zero content on 1.5.6 Moving from entrepreneur to leader and zero on 1.5.4 Forms of business; no other business Unit 1 section in index.json covers either. quizIndices/practiceIndices are assigned sequentially (Block0 q[0], Block1 q[1]+p[0], Block2 q[2]+p[1], Block3 q[3]) not by topic: Block 1 (motives) gets a profit-satisficing MCQ (untaught) and a Define-intrapreneurship practice (Block 0 content); Block 2 (objectives) gets a barriers MCQ and a barriers-to-entry practice (both Block 0 content). Step pairing: Block 1 = (skills, financial) + (non-financial alone); Block 2 = (common objectives, customer/social) + (conflicts alone). The single-section steps mean their recall is shown at the bottom of the step ('immediate') and again at the top of the next step ('spaced') back-to-back — and the two exercises this happens to are the worst ones (the non-orderable motive ranking and the abstract conflict reorder).

Recall design: 5/5 fillins have letter-leaking hints plus templates that paraphrase the body; 6/7 reorders impose order on parallel concepts; all 12 exercises are copies of body flows/bullets rather than transfer tasks; only two shuffle permutations are used across 7 reorders ([2,0,3,1] x3, [3,1,0,2] x3), making the pattern learnable. Three hints have length mismatches vs the answer ('in___________' 13 vs 'independence' 12; 'sa___________' 13 vs 'satisfaction' 12; 'fi________' 10 vs 'financial' 9).

Filler misconceptions: 'the biggest barrier is lack of a good idea' (barriers), 'the best decision is one with no trade-offs' (trade-offs), 'a good manager can achieve all objectives at once' (conflicts) are not things IAL students actually write. The genuine ones are: 'anyone who runs a business is an entrepreneur', 'born not made', 'opportunity cost = money spent', 'all businesses aim to maximise profit', 'social enterprises are charities'.

examMatters is repetitive: 7 of 12 end with a variant of 'always link to the case study context'; none explains the IAL level-mark structure (K/A/An/E) or the 'however/depends on' evaluation moves that WBS11 mark schemes reward.

Duplicate flashcards: the two 'chain' cards ('Trace the chain from an entrepreneur identifying an opportunity...' and 'Trace the impact of different leadership styles...') each appear twice (22 cards, 20 unique fronts).

Notes[] and extras[] cover things content[] does not (profit satisficing, limited liability, sole trader/partnership/Ltd/PLC chain, government support, hard vs soft skills) — students in Learn Mode never see them, while the quiz bank assumes them.

Difficulty ramp and block order are sensible (role -> motives -> objectives -> choices, matching 1.5.1 -> 1.5.2 -> 1.5.3 -> 1.5.5); takeaways match their blocks apart from the 'barriers to entry' wording in Block 0. Zero diagrams is acceptable for this topic but a one-glance 'objective vs life-cycle stage' or 'opportunity cost = next best, not sum' visual would replace the passive fillins.

1.5.6 Moving from entrepreneur to leader: the difficulties in developing from entrepreneur to leader (delegation, trust, loss of control, skill gaps, Greiner-style growth crises) and how to overcome them (training, hiring professional managers, delegation, mentoring) — entirely absent despite the section title.

1.5.4 Forms of business: sole trader, partnership, private limited company; franchising, social enterprise, lifestyle businesses, online businesses; growth to PLC and stock market flotation; limited vs unlimited liability — absent from content (only in extras chains); no other business Unit 1 section covers it.
1.5.1 Anticipating risk and uncertainty in the business environment (risk = quantifiable, uncertainty = not) — not taught.
1.5.2 Financial motives: profit satisficing — not taught in content (only quiz Q1 and a flashcard).

1.5.1 Barriers to entrepreneurship: lack of skills/experience and fear of failure are spec-typical barriers; content lists only finance, competition, red tape, personal risk (the notes[] and flashcards do list them).
Unsure: whether the current WBS11 papers use 'Define' (4 marks) or only 'Explain one' (4 marks) — practice Q0 tariff should be checked against a recent past paper.

Rebuild the practice set for WBS12 scope and IAL tariffs: delete the gearing (idx 1) and ROCE/asset-turnover/dividend-yield (idx 3) questions; add a 4-mark 'Calculate the current ratio and acid test ratio' from a mini statement of financial position, a 4-mark 'Explain one way...', a 10/12-mark 'Assess the internal causes of X's failure', and a 20-mark 'Evaluate whether improving liquidity or profitability should be the priority'; write levels-based guidance that explicitly requires a judgement (remove 'No explicit judgement mark').

Fix the recall layer: remove 3-letter prefix hints on all 7 fill-ins (use word banks with distractors or numeric blanks); delete the duplicate income-statement reorder in net-profit and replace with a numeric profit-ladder fill-in; replace the external-causes 'gradual to sudden' reorder with a causal chain (recession -> income falls -> demand falls -> revenue below fixed costs -> cash exhausted -> closure) or an internal/external sort.

Add the missing spec content as sections: statement of financial position (with a labelled mini example students can extract current assets/liabilities from), working capital and its management, operating profit margin, and a short profit-vs-cash section; introduce the IAL terms 'statement of comprehensive income' and 'profit for the year'; fix the 'Net profit (also called operating profit...)' sentence.

Repair the quiz: reword Q15 to ask for operating profit (or supply interest and tax), rewrite Q19's explanation so it does not claim raising current liabilities improves working capital, dedupe Q5/Q17 and Q9/Q13, replace the three 'Evaluate...' length-giveaway MCQs with content questions on the balance sheet and improving profitability, and remap block 4 quizIndices from [3] to a business-failure item (Q6) and block 3 practiceIndices away from the gearing question.

Correct the Carillion example (it was loss-making, not 'profitable on paper', at collapse), reconcile the 'selling assets' contradiction in the Liquidity block, and add two diagrams (profit waterfall; working capital cycle) since the section currently has none.

Understanding Profit > net-profit > body[0]: 'Net profit (also called operating profit or profit for the year, depending on the level of deduction)' conflates operating profit with net profit. IAL distinguishes operating profit (before interest and tax) from profit for the year (net profit). The section's own flow then says net = after interest and tax, quiz Q0 correctly calls revenue - COS - opex 'operating profit', and Q15 calls the same computation 'net profit'. Three inconsistent messages.

q15: No interest or tax given, so $80,000 is OPERATING profit, not net profit / profit for the year. Q0 labels the identical computation 'operating profit', and the section itself defines net profit as after interest and tax. Directly contradicts the content it tests.

p3: 'Evaluate which financial ratios would be most useful for an investor... (20 marks)' — tariff matches IAL Evaluate, but the model answer is built on ROCE, gearing, asset turnover and dividend yield. Gearing and ROCE are Unit 3 (WBS13 ratio analysis); asset turnover and dividend yield are not on the IAL Business spec at all. None are taught in this section. Guidance is point-allocated (2+3+3+2+2+2+2+2+2) rather than the levels-based scheme IAL uses for 20-markers.

p1: 'Explain two possible reasons why a business might have a high gearing ratio. (6 marks)' — gearing is not in WBS12 2.3 and never appears in content[]; it is also the inline practice shown for the Liquidity block (practiceIndices [1]). But guidance is point-based and states 'No explicit judgement mark' — wrong for IAL: Assess is levels-marked and Level 4 requires a supported judgement/conclusion. Guidance actively steers students away from the thing that earns top level.

Meta number '2.3.3' with title 'Managing Finance' does not match the IAL spec structure: 2.3 is 'Managing finance' with 2.3.1 Profit, 2.3.2 Liquidity, 2.3.3 Business failure. This section bundles all of 2.3 (unsure of exact sub-numbering, confident of the structure).

Duplicate recall on consecutive steps: net-profit's reorder (shown 'spaced' at top of step B) and structure-of-income-statement's reorder (shown 'immediate' at bottom of step C) are the same four income-statement lines.

Blocks 1 ('Understanding Profit') and 2 ('Income Statement') overlap heavily: net-profit already walks the statement top-to-bottom, so block 2 section 1 re-teaches it. Inline quiz mapping is wrong for block 4: quizIndices [3] shows the acid-test MCQ at the end of 'Causes of Business Failure'. No practice question on business failure, the block with the most evaluative potential (typical IAL: 'Assess the likely causes of X's failure' 10/12 marks), and no 'Calculate' question even though IAL Unit 2 routinely asks 4-mark calculate current ratio / acid test / margin from a table.

Zero diagrams for a section that is naturally visual: a revenue -> gross profit -> operating profit -> profit for the year waterfall, and a working capital cycle. Flashcards already contain a working-capital-cycle 'Trace' chain that has no counterpart in content[].

Flashcards and quiz test content not in content[]: statement of financial position, current assets/liabilities definitions, working capital. Learners hit these in free Notes/Flashcards or quiz without ever having been taught them in Learn Mode.
Flashcards 19-21 are exact duplicates of 22-24 (three 'Trace...' cards repeated).
Takeaway for Liquidity block contradicts its own body (sale of underused assets listed as an option in body, forbidden in takeaway/misconception).

Step pairing (gross+net, improve alone; structure+interpreting; understanding+ratios, improving alone; internal+external, why-new alone) is coherent. Difficulty ramp (calculations -> statement -> liquidity -> failure) is sensible.

Misconceptions are mostly real student errors (gross vs net; higher revenue = higher profit; income statement as snapshot; profit = cash; 2:1 rule; bottom-line only). 'Students assume having a good idea is enough' (why-new-businesses) is filler, not an exam misconception.
All seven fill-ins share one design flaw: hints are the first three letters of the answer, so the recall widget tests spelling completion rather than understanding. Systemic, not per-item.

2.3.3 Business failure: internal causes list is reasonable; spec examples such as marketing failure and poor quality are only in flashcards, not content (minor).

Unsure: whether the IAL spec expects calculation of the current/acid test ratios from a supplied statement of financial position — content teaches the formulas but never shows a statement to extract figures from.

Fix the two broken inline quizzes: replace the duplicate '£500' option in quiz[3] (e.g. with -£500 and £3,500) and change content[1].quizIndices from [1] to [8] so the Sales Forecasting block asks a forecasting question.

Add a labelled break-even chart diagram (FC, TC, TR lines; BEP; profit/loss zones; margin of safety) with diagramRef on the Break-Even block, and a cash-flow table diagram for block 3; without them the 'Break-Even Charts' subsection and its reorder are teaching a picture nobody sees.

Rewrite practice[] to IAL shape: a 4-mark 'Calculate' (break-even + margin of safety from given figures), a 2-mark 'What is meant by', a case-anchored 4-mark 'Explain one', a 10-mark 'Assess' and a 20-mark 'Evaluate' with short stimulus extracts, and replace additive points-marking with levels descriptors (K/A/An/E). content.text: q1: Wired as the inline quiz for the 'Sales Forecasting' block (content[1].quizIndices = [1]) before break-even has been taught (block 2). The block has an on-topic question available (Q8, new business with no historical data) that is not used.

q20: Evaluation-as-MCQ: the correct option is the only long, hedged, two-sided one; distractors ('always perfectly accurate', 'useless', 'only manufacturing') are absurd. Answerable by length cue with no knowledge. Same pattern in Q21, Q22, Q24.
q24: Distractors 'They are illegal for businesses to use' and 'They only cover a single day' are not plausible to anyone; question tests nothing.

p0: 'Define the term break-even output (4 marks)'. IAL Business definition questions ('What is meant by...'/'Define') are 2 marks. The 4x1 mark guidance (definition, zero profit, formula, profit/loss zones) is not how a definition is marked; a student trained on this will over-write 2-markers.

p2: 'Assess ... (10 marks)' is a valid IAL allocation, but the guidance is additive points-marking ('2 marks', '1 mark' per point, summing to 10). IAL Business 8/10/12-mark Assess questions are levels-marked (Level 1-4 across Knowledge, Application, Analysis, Evaluation). Also no case-study stimulus is provided for the 'growing restaurant chain', so the Application strand cannot be demonstrated.

p3: 'Evaluate ... (20 marks)' — the 20-mark allocation exists in IAL Business, but the guidance again sums 2-mark points to 20 rather than describing the L1-L4 KAAE levels and the need for a justified judgement. Question is context-free ('business decision-making'); IAL 20-markers are always anchored to the case extract.

p-1: No 'Calculate' question at all (break-even, margin of safety, total contribution, closing balance, variance) despite 4-mark Calculate questions appearing on almost every WBS12 paper. Only 2 of the 5 questions are wired into Learn Mode (practiceIndices on blocks 2 and 3); blocks 0, 1 and 4 get no inline practice even though the budgets question (index 2) and cash-flow question (index 4) exist.

Zero diagrams (content[].diagramRef all null, diagrams = 0) in a section containing a whole subsection 'Break-Even Charts' that describes three lines and an intersection verbally, a reorder recall 'Order the steps to draw a break-even chart', and an examMatters demanding 'precise drawing'. The IAL spec bullet is 'interpretation of break-even charts' — impossible to practise without one. A second diagram (cash-flow table with opening/closing balances) would serve 'cash-flow-forecasts'.

Block 1 'Sales Forecasting' inline MCQ is quizIndices [1] = break-even calculation (LearnModeTab.jsx:106-108 picks it directly). Block 3 'Cash-Flow Forecasting' inline MCQ (quizIndices [3]) has duplicate options. So 2 of the 5 inline quizzes a Learn Mode user sees are broken.

2-per-step pairing: blocks 0, 2, 3 have 3 sections so their second step carries one section plus all block-end widgets (InlineQuiz, InlinePractice, ExplainItBack, Takeaway); blocks 1 and 4 have 2 sections so the entire block, including both NoteSections and all widgets, lands on a single step. Step weight swings from ~1 section to 2 sections + 5 widgets.

Recall placement interacts badly with this section's authoring pattern (every first section has a fillin, every second section has a reorder). Per LearnModeTab.jsx:345-350 and :397-403, the immediate slot always shows currentRecalls[0] (so 8/8 fillins render as immediates, 0 reorders do) and the spaced slot shows the previous step's LAST section recall. Result: profit-and-loss, break-even-evaluation and improving-cash-flow fillins render twice back-to-back (bottom of one step, top of the next), the variance-analysis reorder (last section of last step) never renders, and the 4 other reorders only appear as 'spaced' recalls.

Only two shuffle patterns are used across all five reorders ([2,0,3,1] x3, [3,1,0,2] x2): a student who notices that the third-listed item always goes first can game them. Generate per-recall permutations.

Sequencing: cash-flow forecasting (block 3) is spec 2.3.1 'Planning' content and improving cash flow is 2.3.3 'Liquidity' content; neither neighbouring section covers them (planning-raising-finance has no cash-flow block; managing-finance has 'improving-liquidity'), so keeping them here is defensible but 'improving-cash-flow' now overlaps managing-finance > improving-liquidity. Cross-link rather than duplicate.

Takeaways match their blocks and are accurate; block 2 takeaway correctly restates BEP = FC / contribution. Misconceptions are real student errors (revenue = profit; TC line from origin; favourable = always good; borrow first) rather than filler — this is a strength. Difficulty ramp is sensible (definitions -> calculation -> evaluation) within blocks 2 and 3, but block 1 (forecasting) is entirely descriptive with no calculation or data, and block 4 ends the section on a definition-level note with no calculation practice for variances.
Block 0 realExample emoji for Ocado and Tesco are both the shopping-cart emoji; trivial but shows unreviewed generation.
2.3.2(d) Types of budget: historical figures vs zero-based budgeting — not in content[]; only appears in quiz Q6 and two flashcards.

2.3.2(d) Difficulties of budgeting — touched in one paragraph of purpose-of-budgets (restrictive, discourages initiative) but the standard mark-scheme points (based on forecasts that may be wrong, time-consuming to set, can cause budget-padding/use-it-or-lose-it behaviour, unrealistic targets demotivate) are only in extras.evaluation, not taught.
2.3.2(c) Total contribution (contribution per unit x units sold) and using it to calculate profit (total contribution - fixed costs) — only contribution per unit is taught; no total contribution.
2.3.2(b) Calculation of sales volume vs sales revenue as distinct quantities — 'sales volume' as a term is never used in content (it appears only in common_mistakes).
2.3.2(c) Interpretation of break-even charts — described verbally but with no chart to interpret; effect on BEP of a change in price/FC/VC (a standard IAL question) is not worked through.

2.3.2(a) Difficulties of sales forecasting as a discrete evaluative list (lack of data for new products, market volatility, bias of the forecaster, cost of research) — partially covered under 'accuracy depends on'; unsure whether IAL mark schemes require more than this.
Semi-variable costs and stepped fixed costs — mentioned only in extras.evaluation; unsure whether the IAL spec names semi-variable costs explicitly (Edexcel GCE does).

Add Learn-content blocks for the untaught spec bullets (strategy vs tactics + resource impact; PESTLE + Five Forces; portfolio analysis/BCG + distinctive capabilities), OR remove/quarantine quiz items 3,5,6,7,9 so the pre-test only samples taught material.
Add diagrams for Ansoff's matrix, Porter's strategic matrix (2x2) and the SWOT grid, ideally interactive 'drag this example into the right cell' rather than static images.

Rename 'Porter's Generic Strategies' to 'Porter's Strategic Matrix' and present four cells; fix the Ansoff takeaway to stop ranking product development below market development (and match notes[] which say both are medium risk).

Fix the Netflix SWOT example (password-sharing crackdown is an internal decision, not an external threat; debt weakness is dated) and the Amazon Ansoff example (AWS is diversification, not product development).

Replace the two untaught-topic practice questions with case-applied Ansoff and Porter questions (e.g. 8/10-mark 'Assess whether X should pursue market development or product development'), and attach level-descriptor mark schemes to the 10- and 20-markers.

Strategic Direction > porters-generic-strategies (title, keyIdea, body para 3, block takeaway 'Porter's three strategies'): IAL spec bullet and Edexcel mark schemes use 'Porter's Strategic Matrix' (a 2x2: cost leadership, differentiation, cost focus, differentiation focus). Content presents it as 'Porter's Generic Strategies' with 'three strategies'. Students may not recognise the exam wording, and 'choose one of three' misrepresents the four-cell matrix the spec names.

Corporate Objectives & Strategy > swot-analysis > realExample (Netflix): 'password-sharing crackdowns alienating users' is listed as an external THREAT, but the crackdown is Netflix's own 2023 policy decision (internal), and it in fact drove subscriber growth. Using it as a threat models the exact S/W vs O/T categorisation error the section is trying to teach. 'high debt from original content spend' as a weakness is also dated: Netflix has been strongly free-cash-flow positive since 2022.
q3: BCG/portfolio analysis is never taught in content[] (only in flashcards and notes). Pre-test and inline/post quiz draw from this bank, so students are tested on untaught material.

q5: Genuinely ambiguous: minimum wage is routinely classified as Political (government policy), Economic (labour cost) or Legal in Edexcel resources; the explanation itself concedes 'it could also have economic implications'. Two options are defensible. PESTLE is also not taught in content[].

Only 2 blocks x 2 sections = 2 Learn steps for a spec area (3.1.1-3.1.3) with ~10 bullets; each step is two long reading cards followed by one MCQ, one practice question and ExplainItBack. Very thin for the pre-test/post-test comparison to mean anything.

Zero recall objects (no reorder, no fillin), so Learn Mode has no active-recall widgets at all in this section. The content is grid-based and lends itself to 'classify this example into the correct Ansoff/Porter/SWOT cell' recall rather than reorder.

Zero diagrams for a section whose three core tools are 2x2 matrices (SWOT grid, Ansoff's matrix, Porter's strategic matrix). Students are expected to sketch Ansoff and Porter in the exam; the section never shows them.

Quiz bank mismatch: 5 of 10 MCQs (indices 3,5,6,7,9) test BCG, PESTLE, Five Forces and strategic/tactical decisions, none of which appear in content[]. Types of Change > incremental-vs-disruptive-change > examMatters ('use disruptive change when external forces ... make the current model unsustainable'): Conflates two different concepts. The body defines disruptive change as something that 'comes from outside the established players' and 'destroys incumbents' (Christensen), i.e. a market phenomenon done TO a firm. examMatters then tells the student the firm should 'use disruptive change' as a management choice. A firm cannot 'use' disruption; it undertakes step/transformational change in response to it. The notes[] compound this with 'Disruptive (step) change' and the flashcards switch to 'transformational change', so three vocabularies for one idea.

In IAL 3.6.3 the heading 'Scenario planning' means identifying key risks through risk assessment (natural disasters, IT failure, loss of key staff), planning for risk mitigation (business continuity, succession planning) and the costs/benefits of contingency planning. content[0] 'The Supply Curve' > supply-and-the-supply-curve > realExample: Saudi Arabia is presented as raising output above $80 'because expensive extraction methods become profitable' and cutting drilling when prices fell below $30 in early 2016. Saudi Arabia has the lowest lifting costs in the world (roughly $3-10/bbl) and its output is set by OPEC/political strategy; in 2014-16 it famously INCREASED production to record levels (~10.5m bpd) to defend market share while prices collapsed. The example describes US shale/oil-sands behaviour and attributes it to the wrong producer; a student who repeats it in an exam is writing something a well-informed examiner knows is false.

The WEC11 supply/PES bullet only requires 'the distinction between short run and long run and its significance for elasticity of supply'. q21: correctIndex 0 ('market price exceeds its average total costs') is wrong or at best contestable. A firm continues to supply in the short run as long as price covers average VARIABLE cost (shut-down rule) and produces where P = MC; option 1 ('price is at least equal to its marginal cost') is the textbook supply condition for a price-taking firm. P > ATC is the long-run break-even condition, and a firm with P < ATC but P > AVC still supplies. This is WEC13 Unit 3 theory-of-the-firm content anyway and has no place in a WEC11 supply bank; it can be drawn into the PreTest at random.

Guidance gives evaluation 1 mark, which does not match a 10-mark level scheme; and via the sort bug this question lands on Block 5 rather than the YED block.

Practice-to-block mapping is broken: LearnModeTab.jsx builds sortedPractice (sorted by marks) and indexes practiceIndices into it, but the JSON's practiceIndices were authored against the unsorted array. Result: Block 1 (Demand Curve) gets 'Define PED', Block 2 (PED) gets 'Outline EV demand shift', Block 3 (YED) gets 'Explain PED factors', Block 5 gets 'Analyse YED'; the 20-mark Evaluate never shows.

Diagrams 'PED Values: Visual Comparison' and 'YED and XED Interpretation' never render in Learn Mode: Block 2 diagramRef 'PED' first-matches 'PED and Total Revenue' (LearnModeTab.jsx:97-104), and Blocks 3/4 have diagramRef null. Half the diagram set is invisible in the primary flow.

Every block has exactly 3 sections, so 2-per-step pairing yields a 2-section step then a 1-section step in every block; the 1-section step then carries diagram + quiz + practice + Explain-It-Back + takeaway + spaced recall + immediate recall — the heaviest step is always the shortest reading, and the rhythm is identical six times.
Inline quiz only ever uses quiz indices 0-7 (quizIndices per block); indices 8-24 are reachable only via pre/post-test and the paywalled Quiz tab.

Block 5 'Significance of Elasticities' largely repeats 'Significance of YED' and 'Significance of XED' subsections already in Blocks 3-4; its reorder recall is a recap of the block's own paragraph order.

Diminishing marginal utility (Block 0) is never connected to the downward-sloping demand curve (Block 1), so the two halves of the section do not link — the spec's reason for teaching DMU here is missing.
Fill-in word banks contain only the answers (FillInRecall.jsx:12), so every fill-in is an n-item matching puzzle with no distractors; two are uncompletable because of duplicate answers.

Filler misconceptions: 'students treat elasticities as purely theoretical' (using-elasticities-for-business-decisions), 'firms should only sell necessities' (significance-of-yed), 'XED only matters for substitutes' (significance-of-xed) are invented rather than observed marking errors; the genuine ones (demand vs Qd, total vs marginal utility, inferior ≠ low quality, price as a shifter, sign of YED) are good.
Several 'flow' blocks present parallel effects as sequences (demand-and-the-demand-curve: 'Income effect → Substitution effect'), reinforcing the same false-sequence habit the reorders have.

examMatters repeatedly asserts paper frequency ('almost every paper', 'often open a paper', 'a common 8-mark question') that does not match WEC11's structure; students in international schools will take these as fact.
Diminishing marginal utility as the explanation for the downward slope of the demand curve (spec links DMU to the shape of the demand curve) — DMU is taught but never applied to the curve.
'Conditions of demand' as the spec term for shift factors — not used; students should recognise the phrase in questions.
PED varying along a straight-line demand curve (elastic above midpoint, inelastic below) — only in a diagram and quiz[7], not in content body.
Significance of elasticities for CONSUMERS (spec: firms, consumers and government) — diagram 3 checklist promises it, content covers only firms and government.
Calculating elasticities from a data table/diagram (IAL routinely gives P/Q tables) — worked example only in prose flows; no table-based practice.

Unsure: exact WEC11 1.3.2 bullet list — if elasticities are a separate spec point the section may be over-packed; if behavioural economics is absent from WEC11 (likely), Block 0 subsection 3 is off-spec.

Fix quiz Q18 (key it to 'MSC and MSB/D from Qopt to Qm') and extras.chains[0]; delete duplicates Q11/Q12/Q19/Q9; then remap quizIndices and practiceIndices so each block's inline MCQ/practice is on-topic (currently blocks 4-7 get the wrong questions and the monopolist Q7 is unused).

Fix the Learn Mode diagram wiring: change block 7 diagramRef from 'Deadweight Loss' to something that matches (or retitle a diagram), add a diagramRef for the Positive Externality of Consumption diagram (spec-required, currently never shown), add 'Merit' ref for block 4; relabel SVG axes 'Costs, Benefits' and Qe->Qm.

Correct the four teaching errors: public goods 'zero quantity / complete failure' (contradicts own common_mistakes and spec 'may not be provided'); the lighthouse example (privately funded via light dues — the classic counterexample); measuring-welfare-loss para 1 (competitive equilibrium is not the optimum under an externality); 'examiners penalise MSC>MPC for a consumption externality'; plus practice[1] attributing free riding to non-rivalry and 'mandatory insurance' filed under moral hazard.

Re-scope to WEC11: add short subsections on symmetric vs asymmetric information, private vs public vs quasi-public goods, and the social = private + external identity; move Market Power (Unit 3) and Moral Hazard/Adverse Selection (Unit 4) into an 'extension' block or out of the section; merge the three deadweight-loss subsections into one.

Rebuild the recalls: stop copying the flow box verbatim (or show reorders only as 'spaced' on the next step); remove first-letter hints or accept synonyms (overconsumes/overproduces, more/better/superior, optimal/competitive); fix the five wrong-length hints; replace the two non-sequential reorders (what-is-market-failure, merit-goods) and the pseudo-procedure (measuring-welfare-loss) with classify tasks or a numeric welfare-loss calculation.

Public Goods > characteristics-public-goods (body para 4) and block takeaway 'Private markets produce zero public goods — complete failure': Absolutist claim that the free market provides 'zero quantity' of public goods. The IAL spec wording is 'why public goods MAY NOT be provided by the private sector'. The section's own common_mistakes[2] ('Saying public goods cannot be provided by the market') says this exact claim is a mistake and that the issue is under-provision. Internal contradiction that a student will be marked down for repeating.

Public Goods > characteristics-public-goods > realExample (UK lighthouse system): States lighthouses were 'historically funded by the government' and that Trinity House 'collects dues from ports rather than individual vessels'. Historically English lighthouses were largely privately built and financed by light dues levied on ships (Coase 1974 uses this as the canonical counterexample of private provision of a public good); today light dues are charged per ship tonnage on vessels calling at UK/Irish ports into the General Lighthouse Fund, not general taxation. The example undermines the point it is meant to make and is factually wrong.

Welfare Loss & Deadweight Loss > measuring-welfare-loss (body para 1): 'In a perfectly competitive market, total surplus is maximised at the equilibrium where supply meets demand. Any deviation from this point — whether through externalities, monopoly power, or government intervention — reduces total surplus.' With an externality the market equilibrium is NOT the surplus-maximising point; the externality is a property of that equilibrium, not a deviation from it, and moving away from it (a Pigouvian tax) raises welfare. This contradicts the whole Externalities block and the practice[3] model answer.

Externalities > negative-externalities-consumption > examMatters: 'Examiners penalise students who draw MSC above MPC for a consumption externality.' Edexcel/IAL mark schemes for demerit-good/cigarette questions routinely accept an external-cost (MSC > MPC) diagram; the IAL spec only requires diagrams for external costs of production and external benefits of consumption. Telling students they will be penalised for the diagram most mark schemes list is misleading about marking.

q18: The keyed answer 'The area between the MSC and MPC curves, up to the free market quantity' is WRONG: that area (MSC-MPC from 0 to Qm) is the total external cost, not the welfare loss. Q5 in the same bank explicitly keys the correct answer as 'MSC and MPB from Qopt to Qm' and labels 'MPC and MSC from 0 to Qm' as a distractor meaning 'total external cost'. Q18's own explanation ('from the socially optimal quantity to the free market quantity') contradicts its option text. A pre-test can draw Q5 and Q18 together and mark opposite things right.
content.evidence: audit/snapshots/2026-09-11-post-packet-0__economics__market-failure.json quiz[18].options[0] and explanation rewritten to the MSC/MSB triangle from Qopt to Qm, no longer keys the MSC-MPC external-cost area as welfare loss

content.text: p1: 'Explain two reasons why public goods would not be provided by the free market (6 marks)' is realistic in size, but the model answer is wrong on mechanism: it attributes the free-rider problem to non-RIVALRY ('Reason 2: Non-rivalry ... This leads to the free-rider problem'). Free riding is caused by non-excludability, as the content itself says (free-rider-problem body para 1). A student copying this scores less than the guidance claims. Also 'would not be provided' hard-codes the absolutist claim.

quizIndices are sequential (block n -> quiz n) rather than topical, so Learn Mode's inline MCQ is off-topic for four blocks: 'Merit Goods & Demerit Goods' gets Q3 (free rider), 'Information Failures' gets Q4 (merit goods), 'Market Power' gets Q5 (negative production externality welfare-loss area), 'Welfare Loss & Deadweight Loss' gets Q6 (moral hazard). Q7 (monopolist) is never used. Suggested: Public Goods [2,3], Merit [4,8,14], Info Failures [6,15], Market Power [7], Welfare Loss [5,18-fixed,21].

practiceIndices are similarly misaligned for the last two blocks: 'Market Power' -> practice[3] (Evaluate taxation for negative production externalities), 'Welfare Loss' -> practice[4] (Outline information failure examples). No monopoly or welfare-loss practice question exists.

Block 7 diagramRef 'Deadweight Loss' matches no diagram title (titles: 'Negative Externality of Production', 'Positive Externality of Consumption', 'Public Goods & the Free-Rider Problem', 'Merit & Demerit Goods'), so the InlineDiagram for the diagram-heaviest block renders nothing. Block 2 diagramRef 'Negative Externality' only matches diagrams[0], so the 'Positive Externality of Consumption' diagram (a spec-required diagram) is never shown in Learn Mode; block 4 (Merit/Demerit) has no diagramRef although a matching diagram exists.

Every one of the 8 reorder recalls is the subsection's own flow box (steps + result) verbatim, and the 'immediate' recall renders at the bottom of the same step where that flow box is visible. It is a copy-from-screen task, not retrieval. All 8 fillins carry first-letters+underscore hints that make the blank one-option; 5 hints have the wrong length (allocative-inefficiency 'un____________', free-rider 'ex_________' and 'ta_______', demerit 'ex____________', diagrams-welfare-loss 'un____________' and 'co__________').

Redundant coverage: 'allocative-inefficiency-deadweight-loss' (block 1) and 'measuring-welfare-loss' + 'diagrams-welfare-loss' (block 7) teach the same deadweight-loss idea three times, with block 1 introducing DWL before the student has seen a single externality diagram. Merge block 7 into block 2 (externality welfare loss) and cut block 1 to a definition + the three spec types.

Difficulty ramp/spec fit: blocks 4 (merit/demerit), 5b (moral hazard/adverse selection) and 6 (monopoly) are Unit 3/4 or non-Edexcel material yet sit in the middle of the Unit 1 section; a WEC11 student is told 'examiners expect you to draw a monopoly diagram', which is not examined in Unit 1. Meanwhile the spec's 1.3.4 'symmetric vs asymmetric information' and 1.3.3 'public vs private goods' get no subsection.

2-per-step pairing is coherent (neg prod + neg cons; pos prod + pos cons; merit + demerit; then info failure alone; asymmetric + moral hazard; monopoly alone; measuring + diagrams). No pairing breaks a concept.

Takeaways mostly match their blocks; exceptions: Public Goods takeaway 'Private markets produce zero public goods — complete failure' contradicts common_mistakes[2]; Externalities takeaway 'Government uses taxes and subsidies to close the gap' is the only mention of intervention in a block that otherwise never teaches it.

Misconceptions: most are genuine (public goods = government-provided; education is a public good; merit vs public; moral hazard vs adverse selection; DWL vs fall in consumer surplus; allocative vs productive inefficiency). Filler-ish: 'negative externalities only come from pollution', 'information failure only affects uneducated consumers', 'free riding = laziness', 'monopolies are always bad' (the last is Unit 3 evaluation, not a Unit 1 misconception).

Pre-test gate draws 3 random MCQs from a 25-item bank that contains a wrongly keyed item (Q18), four near-duplicate pairs and two untaught topics (Q20, Q22); a student can be told they were wrong for a correct answer before the lesson even starts.
1.3.4(a) 'distinction between symmetric and asymmetric information' — symmetric information is never defined or contrasted; only asymmetric is taught.
1.3.3(a) 'distinction between public goods and private goods' — private goods (rival, excludable) are never defined; quasi-public goods / common resources are not taught although quiz Q20 tests them.

1.3.2(a)/(b) explicit 'private cost + external cost = social cost' and 'private benefit + external benefit = social benefit' relationships are only in common_mistakes[0] and quiz Q16, never stated as a taught formula in a subsection body.
1.3.2(d) welfare GAIN from correcting a positive consumption externality (spec wording covers welfare loss and gain areas); content only ever calls the positive-externality triangle a 'welfare loss'.

Unit 1 numbering: the app labels this '1.3.5 Market Failure'; in the 2018 IAL spec market failure is 1.3.1-1.3.4 (types, externalities, public goods, information gaps) — unsure of the app's mapping convention; worth checking that 1.3.1-1.3.4 are not double-covered elsewhere.

Not spec gaps but over-coverage worth flagging: merit/demerit goods (not Edexcel terminology in IAL Unit 1), monopoly as market failure (WEC13 Unit 3), moral hazard/adverse selection (WEC14 Unit 4 financial market failure).

Re-map quizIndices to block content (e.g. block0 [0,12,14,23]; block1 [6,15,9]; block2 [1,10]; block3 [2,11,17]; block4 [3,16]; block5 [8,20,24]; block6 [7,19]; block7 [4,5,13,18,22]) and fix practiceIndices so each block gets its own question — either index the marks-sorted array deliberately or remove the sort in LearnModeTab.jsx:82 before indexing. Put the essay on block 7.

Change block 0 diagramRef from 'Indirect Tax' to a string contained in the diagram title (e.g. 'Tax to Correct') so the tax diagram renders; consider adding a specific-vs-ad-valorem supply-shift diagram.

Stop reorder recalls duplicating the on-screen flow: either render the first section's recall only as a spaced recall on the next step, or rewrite the nine reorders as longer chains (incidence, revenue, elasticity, Pc/Pp) that are not visible above. Replace the three weak reorders (direct-state-provision, types-of-regulation, examples-and-evaluation) with the free-rider chain, a classification exercise, and a scenario judgement.

Fix practice mark allocations to WEC11 format: 20-mark Evaluate -> 14-mark 'Discuss'/'Evaluate' with a KAA/Evaluation level split in the guidance; 4-mark Define -> 2-mark Define or 4-mark 'Explain, with an example'; 'Outline' -> 'Explain'. Rewrite guidance as levels, not point sums.

Correct the factual/IAL-fit issues: London taxi example (no numeric cap), MUP '13% in the first year', plug-in grant 'up to £1,500', 'UK airline deregulation', nudge-theory exam claim; add the spec-named government-failure causes (distortion of price signals, excessive administrative costs) and swap several UK examples for international ones.

Government Failure > examples-and-evaluation-of-government-failure > realExample: Claims London taxi licensing 'restricted the number of black cabs', 'keeping fares high and limiting supply'. London has never numerically capped black-cab licences (the constraint is the Knowledge test; fares are set by TfL). The capped-medallion case is New York, not London. Students citing this in an exam would be citing a false fact.

State Provision > information-provision-and-nudge-theory > examMatters: 'Nudge theory is increasingly popular in exam questions ... libertarian paternalism' — nudge theory and libertarian paternalism are not in the IAL WEC11 specification (1.2.10 covers habitual behaviour, influence of others, computational weakness). This is UK GCE-flavoured content presented as an IAL exam expectation.

p3: 'Evaluate ... (20 marks)' — 20-mark essays are WEC13/WEC14 (Unit 3/4) format. WEC11 Section B tops out at 14 marks (Discuss/Evaluate). Guidance is also point-allocated (2+3+2+2+2+2+2+1+2+2) whereas IAL uses levels-based KAA + Evaluation marking. In addition this question is never surfaced in Learn Mode because practiceIndices only reach sorted positions 0-3.

quizIndices are sequential [0]..[7] and do not match block content: block 'Subsidies' shows Q1 (maximum price), 'Maximum Prices' shows Q2 (minimum price on alcohol), 'Minimum Prices' shows Q3 (permits vs tax), 'Tradeable Pollution Permits' shows Q4 (government failure definition), 'State Provision' shows Q5 (rent controls as government failure), 'Regulation' shows Q6 (vaccination subsidy). Only blocks 0 (Q0 tax) and 7 (Q7 regulatory capture) are on-topic. Six of eight inline quizzes are off-topic.

practiceIndices are applied to a marks-sorted copy of practice[] (LearnModeTab.jsx:82 sortedPractice, :110-113), so the data indices [0],[1],[2],[3] resolve to: block 'Subsidies' -> 'Define government failure' (worked mode), 'Minimum Prices' -> 'Outline two disadvantages of a maximum price' (guided), 'State Provision' -> 'Explain two ways indirect taxes correct market failure' (guided), 'Government Failure' -> 'Assess subsidies' (independent). Every inline practice is in the wrong block, and the 20-mark essay never appears. Either the data must index the sorted array deliberately or the code must stop sorting before indexing.

diagramRef 'Indirect Tax' on block 0 never matches diagram title 'Tax to Correct Negative Externality' (LearnModeTab.jsx:97-104 requires one string to contain the other), so the tax diagram — the one the section's examMatters says 'examiners expect you to draw' — is never rendered in Learn Mode. The other three refs (Subsidy, Maximum Price, Minimum Price) match.

All nine reorder recalls are verbatim copies of the flow widget in the same section's body, and because each is the first section of its step they render as 'immediate' recalls at the bottom of the same step with the flow visible above. Students can copy the order from the screen; the reorder score in CompletionScreen is therefore meaningless for this section.

Fill-in recalls are a three-word drag bank (FillInRecall.jsx:12). With three grammatically distinct slots, six of eight are solved by grammar without economics. 'Complete the chain:' is used for lists that are not chains (price floors: income/store/wage; causes of government failure: imperfect/short-termism/capture).
Six hint strings are one character longer than the answer (opportunity, information, architecture, competition, imperfect, short-termism) — cosmetic but signals unreviewed generation.

Step structure is monotone: nine steps, each 'How X works' + 'Evaluating X' + MCQ + takeaway + explain-back. There is no ramp; every policy tool is treated at the same depth, and the section never asks students to choose between tools for a given market failure (the actual IAL 12/14-mark skill) until the final block.

Real examples are almost entirely UK (tobacco duty, sugar levy, plug-in grant, NHS, National Minimum Wage, Scotland MUP, UK auto-enrolment, UK buses/airlines, London taxis). For an IAL cohort in HK/SG/MY/PK/LK/Middle East, IAL papers use international contexts; examples like Singapore COE, Malaysian/Indonesian fuel subsidies, India MSP floors, Pakistan wheat support prices, HK public housing would land better.

Misconception filler: 'Maximum Prices > effects-and-evaluation-of-price-ceilings > misconception' ('students assume the government should set it closer to equilibrium') describes a legitimate trade-off, not a misconception; the text concedes the point. Most other misconceptions are genuine (permits 'rich firms pollute as much as they want', 'subsidies always better than taxes', 'information always works').

Block 7 pairing: step 8 = 'What is government failure' + 'Causes'; step 9 = 'Examples and Evaluation' alone. Coherent, but step 9 is where the 20-mark essay should sit and it currently receives 'Assess subsidies' instead.
Takeaways match their blocks. Block 2 takeaway 'Subsidies may achieve affordability without creating shortages' is only supported by one sentence of examMatters, not the body.

Government failure causes named in the IAL spec: 'distortion of price signals' is never stated as a cause (the section lists imperfect information, political short-termism, regulatory capture, unintended consequences); 'excessive administrative costs' is only mentioned in passing in examples-and-evaluation, not taught as a cause.

Tax incidence on consumers vs producers (specific and ad valorem) is referenced in examMatters and tested in Q23 but never taught; the section needs at least a cross-reference to 1.2.9 or a short incidence paragraph tied to the tax diagram's Pc/Pp labels.
Specific vs ad valorem taxes: mentioned in one sentence (parallel vs pivotal shift) with no diagram; the spec expects students to draw both.
Minimum price on demerit goods vs indirect tax comparison (who receives the extra revenue: retailers vs government) — a standard IAL evaluation point, absent.

Choosing between interventions for a given market failure (e.g. tax vs regulation vs permits for pollution; subsidy vs state provision vs information for a merit good) is only partially covered in permits and regulation examMatters; no dedicated comparison content.

Spec numbering: unsure whether IAL 2018 places government failure under 1.3.6 or a separate point; the section merges both, which is defensible, but worth confirming against the WEC11 specification document.
Buffer stock schemes appear in the quiz (Q21) but are not in the section and, as far as I recall, not in the 2018 IAL WEC11 spec — unsure; if they are, they need teaching; if not, remove Q21.

Add tax and subsidy diagrams (specific parallel shift, ad valorem pivot, consumer/producer incidence shares, tax revenue rectangle, subsidy cost rectangle) and give them titles that the diagramRef substring match will find ('Indirect Tax', 'Subsidy'), so Blocks 4 and 5 stop rendering with no diagram.

Rebuild practice[] to the IAL Appendix 6 tariffs (Define 2 / Explain 4 / Draw 4 / Calculate 2-4 / Analyse 6 / Examine 8 / Discuss 14 / Evaluate 20): delete the UK oil-price macro essay and the 'Outline' price-floor item, add a Calculate on incidence/revenue, a Draw on a subsidy, and an Examine/Discuss on the price mechanism across local/national/global markets; make practiceIndices index practice[] (not the marks-sorted copy) so each block gets an on-topic question.

Fix the recall layer: give every fillin a word bank with distractors (elastic/inelastic, up/down, left/right, demand/supply, original/new) and remove first-letter hints; replace the five non-sequence reorders (equilibrium slopes, producer surplus $150/$200, three price-mechanism functions, tax welfare areas, subsidy evaluation) with classification or diagram-area drills.

Teach the missing spec bullets - 3b price mechanism in local, national and global markets (with Asian/Middle-East examples) and 2b effect of demand/supply shifts on CS and PS - then re-key Q14 to the standard answer; move Block 6 to 1.3.2 and re-key it to the spec's own list (herding, habit, inertia, poor computation, need to feel valued, framing/bias).

Correct or replace the wrong/dated examples (London 'rent controls', CBO sugar-tax score, Glastonbury resale, 59p fuel duty, pre-2003 CAP) and de-UK the examples for the HK/SG/MY/PK audience; fix quizIndices so the CS/PS block shows Q6 and the Subsidies block shows a subsidy MCQ.

Equilibrium Price & Quantity > excess-demand-and-excess-supply > realExample: Claims London has 'rent controls' that keep supply below equilibrium. Private-sector rent control in England was abolished by the Housing Act 1988; London rents are market-set. Also 'many are outbid' describes price adjusting upward, which contradicts the claim of below-equilibrium pricing.

Consumer Surplus & Producer Surplus > total-welfare-and-efficiency > realExample: 'The US Congressional Budget Office estimates deadweight loss when scoring tax proposals. A proposed sugar tax...' - CBO scores federal legislation and does not publish deadweight-loss triangles in scores; there is no federal sugar-tax score of this kind. Worse, the example contradicts the paragraph's own misconception text: a sugar tax targets a negative externality, so it can raise, not reduce, total welfare.

q14: Keyed answer 'ambiguous' conflicts with (a) the section's own teaching ('When the price rises, consumer surplus shrinks' in consumer-surplus body[1], which points students to 'decreases') and (b) the standard IAL answer for spec bullet 2b: with a rightward demand shift and upward-sloping supply, the CS triangle under the new demand curve is larger, so CS rises. Three contradictory signals on a spec-listed point.

p3: 'Evaluate the impact of a significant increase in global oil prices on the UK economy (20 marks)' is a Unit 2 (WEC12) macro essay: the guidance is entirely cost-push inflation, real disposable income, GDP growth and Bank of England monetary policy - none of it taught in 1.3.4, and UK-specific for international students. The 20-mark tariff itself matches IAL 'Evaluate', but the guidance is point-marked ('3 marks', '2 marks') whereas IAL 20-markers are levels-marked (KAA + evaluation levels).

content.text: p2: 'Assess the effectiveness of the price mechanism... (10 marks)': 'Assess' is not an IAL Economics command word (spec Appendix 6 lists Define 2, Calculate 2/4, Draw 4, Explain 4, Analyse 6, Examine 8, Discuss 14, Evaluate 20) and there is no 10-mark tariff in WEC11. The guidance is point-marked, not levels-marked. Should be 'Examine... (8)' or 'Discuss... (14)', ideally with reference to an extract, and should mention local/national/global markets (spec 3b).

p4: 'Outline two effects of a price floor set above the equilibrium price (4 marks)': 'Outline' is not an IAL command word, and price floors/minimum wage are 1.3.6 Government intervention, not taught in this section's content (only flashcards mention them). Model answer's 'government may need to purchase surplus output' is fine but off-topic here.

p2: Bank-level gap: none of the five questions covers indirect taxes, subsidies, incidence, or CS/PS (half the spec bullets), and there is no Calculate or Draw question despite the QS requirement (>=20% of marks) and the topic being the most diagram-heavy in Unit 1. Additionally LearnModeTab.jsx:80/113 indexes practiceIndices into the marks-sorted list, so Block 3 (Price Mechanism) shows the price-floor question and Block 4 (Indirect Taxes) shows the excess-supply question; the Assess and Evaluate items never appear inline.

No diagram renders for the Indirect Taxes or Subsidies blocks: diagramRef 'Indirect Tax' and 'Subsidy' are matched by substring against diagram titles ('Supply & Demand Equilibrium', 'Consumer & Producer Surplus') in LearnModeTab.jsx:97-104, so neither matches; and no tax/subsidy/incidence/DWL SVG exists anywhere in diagrams[]. Meanwhile examMatters in three subsections tells students tax/subsidy diagrams are compulsory.

Inline quiz mismatch: quizIndices [1] puts Q1 (increase in demand) on the Consumer/Producer Surplus block instead of Q6; quizIndices [4] puts Q4 (cigarette tax incidence) on the Subsidies block instead of Q5/Q13/Q20; the Alternative Views block has no quizIndices although Q7 (bounded rationality) exists.

Inline practice mismatch (practiceIndices index the marks-sorted array): Price Mechanism block gets 'Outline two effects of a price floor'; Indirect Taxes block gets 'Explain excess supply -> equilibrium'; the Assess and Evaluate questions are never surfaced.

2-per-step pairing leaves singleton steps that carry all block widgets: Block 1 = [how-markets, excess-demand] + [changes-in-equilibrium alone + diagram + quiz + practice + explain + takeaway]; Block 2 = [CS, PS] + [total-welfare alone + widgets]; Block 4 = [specific/ad-valorem, incidence] + [welfare-effects alone + widgets]. The heaviest steps are the ones with the least content, and the 'spaced' recall shown at the top of those steps is the previous step's weak reorder (e.g. the producer-surplus $150/$200 ordering).

Block 6 'Alternative Views of Consumer & Producer Behaviour' is misplaced: in the IAL spec it is 1.3.2(1b) 'Reasons why consumers may not aim to maximise utility' with a fixed list (herding, habitual behaviour, inertia, poor computational skills, need to feel valued, framing and bias). The block instead teaches anchoring, loss aversion, availability heuristic, nudges and Simon's bounded rationality, has no diagram, quiz or practice, and reads as an appendix.

Content weighting vs spec: two subsections on deadweight-loss welfare analysis (total-welfare-and-efficiency, welfare-effects-of-taxation) and one on the invisible hand are not IAL 1.3.4 bullets, while spec 3b (price mechanism in local, national and global markets) and 2b (how changes in demand/supply affect CS and PS) have no subsection at all.

Forward references: effects-and-evaluation-of-subsidies (body[0], recall) depends on 'positive externality' and 'socially optimal level', which are 1.3.5 concepts; total-welfare-and-efficiency introduces 'allocative efficiency' without the 1.3.5 framing.

Misconceptions: most are genuine (movement vs shift, CS is not 'saving', PS is not profit, ad valorem drawn parallel, subsidy shifts supply up, tax revenue is not a welfare loss, bounded rationality is not irrationality). Two are exam-technique tips dressed as misconceptions: signalling-incentive-rationing ('Students list the three functions but fail to explain') and behavioural-economics ('proves people are irrational').

Meta says mistakes: 0 but common_mistakes[] has 3 good entries (adjustment process, CS/PS labelling, marking the new equilibrium) - these are not surfaced in Learn Mode. Flashcards include price ceilings/floors/black markets (1.3.6 content).

Takeaways match their blocks and are accurate; difficulty ramp (equilibrium -> surplus -> mechanism -> tax -> subsidy) is sensible, with welfare tools introduced in Block 2 before being reused in Block 4.
1.3.4 3(b) The price mechanism in the context of different types of markets, including local, national and global markets - not taught anywhere (no subsection, no example, no recall, no MCQ).

1.3.4 2(b) How changes in demand or supply might affect consumer and producer surplus - only a one-line 'when price falls the triangle gets bigger'; no diagram of a shift's effect on CS/PS, and the one MCQ on it (Q14) is keyed 'ambiguous'.

1.3.4 4(d) The incidence of subsidies on consumers and producers - one sentence ('split depends on relative elasticities'); no rule stated (inelastic demand -> consumers capture more of the subsidy), no diagram, no recall; only Q20 tests it numerically.

Remove the 10 off-topic GDP-measurement MCQs (indices 12-16, 18, 20-23) from this section's bank (move to 2.1.1) so the pre-test and inline quizzes only test what the section teaches; then re-point quizIndices so multiplier calculations (1, 3, 5) sit on block 4 and classification/equilibrium items (0, 4, 2/6, 9, 11) sit on blocks 1-3.

content.text: Repair diagramRefs: set content[2].diagramRef to match a new AD/AS 'Equilibrium real national output' diagram (price level / real output axes) and content[3].diagramRef to 'Injections and Withdrawals Equilibrium' (whose ΔY > ΔJ scenario is the multiplier picture), so blocks 3 and 4 actually show a diagram.

content[0] The Circular Flow of Income > three-sector-model > examMatters; and content[1] > injections-explained > body[0]: Teaches that transfer payments are government spending (G) and an injection ('these are government spending (injection) even though they are not payment for output'; 'Government spending (G) is expenditure on public services, infrastructure, and transfer payments').
