content.text: q12: Off-topic: GDP measurement methods are not taught anywhere in this section's content[] blocks, yet the question can be drawn into the 3-question pre-test. Same for indices 15, 16, 18, 21, 22, 23 (income method, NNI, PPP, real vs nominal, output method, GDP per capita) and 20 (stock vs flow). 10 of 24 MCQs test untaught material.
q1: Question is fine; placement is not. quizIndices for block 2 ('Injections and Withdrawals') = [1,2], so this multiplier calculation is the inline quiz two blocks before the multiplier is taught.

q3: Same sequencing problem: block 3 ('Equilibrium National Income') quizIndices = [3], so the second multiplier calculation is shown before block 4 teaches the multiplier. Meanwhile block 4's inline quiz is quiz[4] (basic I/G/X vs S/T/M classification) — too easy for the multiplier block — and quiz[5] (which factor shrinks the multiplier) is never shown because only the first unused index is used.

p1: 'Explain two reasons why national income figures may not accurately reflect the standard of living (6 marks)' — this is 2.1.1 (measures of economic performance / limitations of GDP), not circular flow / equilibrium / multiplier. Because practice is sorted by marks in LearnModeTab.jsx:80, this lands as the inline practice for block 3 'Equilibrium National Income' where it is irrelevant.
p-1: No practice question requires a diagram (J/W or AD/AS) or a multiplier calculation with given MPS/MPT/MPM, which are the two most common ways IAL Unit 2 tests this topic.

Heavy redundancy: content[0] section 'three-sector-model' already teaches all three injections, all three withdrawals and the J = W equilibrium rule in full; content[1] then re-teaches 'Injections: I, G, X', 'Withdrawals: S, T, M' and 'The Injections-Withdrawals Balance' as three separate sections. A student reads the same takeaway ('Injections (I, G, X) add to the flow; withdrawals (S, T, M) leak out') at the end of block 1 and again at the end of block 2.

content[2] 'planned-vs-actual' and 'adjustment-to-equilibrium' are the same mechanism told twice (excess demand → inventories fall; excess supply → inventories rise). Merge into one section with both directions and use the freed slot for the AD/AS equilibrium diagram the spec expects.

Broken diagramRefs: content[2].diagramRef = 'National Income Equilibrium' and content[3].diagramRef = 'The Multiplier' match no diagram title ('Circular Flow of Income', 'Injections and Withdrawals Equilibrium') under the bidirectional substring match in LearnModeTab.jsx:97-104. Blocks 3 and 4 therefore render no InlineDiagram; the J/W diagram with its 'ΔY > ΔJ' multiplier scenario is shown at block 2, before the multiplier exists.

Inline quiz sequencing (quizIndices): block 2 → quiz[1] (multiplier calc), block 3 → quiz[3] (multiplier calc), block 4 → quiz[4] (basic classification). Calculations appear two blocks before the concept; the multiplier block gets the easiest question; quiz[2] and quiz[5] are never surfaced.

Pre-test draws 3 random MCQs from a 24-item bank in which 10 items test GDP-measurement content (2.1.1) never taught in this section — a plausible driver of the 'pre-test demotivates' feedback and of step-0 abandonment.

Step pairing: block 2 (3 sections) and block 4 (3 sections) leave a single-section final step carrying diagram + quiz + practice + explain-back + takeaway + two recall widgets — the heaviest step in the section is anchored by the shortest content. Block 1 and 3 (2 sections each) are one step each, so the section has 6 steps but 4 block-end widget dumps.
Takeaways match their blocks, but content[0].takeaway[1-2] duplicate content[1].takeaway[0-2] almost verbatim.

Misconceptions: 'savings as injection / investment as withdrawal', 'investment vs financial investment', 'I = S, G = T, X = M must each hold', 'identity vs equilibrium', 'multiplier is a fixed number', and 'MPC must exclude tax/imports' are genuine and well-phrased. 'Students treat the circular flow as a description of reality' and 'Students describe the adjustment as instantaneous' are filler — not errors students actually make in exams.

Difficulty ramp inside prose is sensible (model → J/W → equilibrium → multiplier → evaluation), but the section never connects to AD/AS: the multiplier is not explicitly linked to the size of an AD shift (spec bullet), and 'equilibrium real national output' is only shown via J/W and Keynesian-cross narrative, never on price-level/real-output axes.

Distinction between income and wealth (flow vs stock) — quiz[20] tests it but no content[] section teaches it (unsure whether IAL keeps the UK 2.4.1 wording, but it appears in IAL textbooks for this topic).

Equilibrium level of real national output shown on an AD/AS diagram (price level vs real output) and using AD/AS to show how the economy moves toward equilibrium — no AD/AS diagram or explanation in this section; equilibrium is treated only through injections/withdrawals and the inventory mechanism.
Significance of the multiplier for shifts in AD (the multiplied horizontal shift of AD) — only implied by quiz[8]; not taught in content[3].

The multiplier ratio as change in real income / change in injection, with calculations from given data (e.g. given ΔY and ΔG, find k) — only the k = 1/MPW direction is drilled; the ratio definition appears only in notes[3] and practice[2] guidance.

Note: the app numbers this 2.3.4 and the notes cross-reference 2.3.2 (AD), 2.3.5 (output gap), 2.3.6 (fiscal policy); I am unsure this matches the official WEC12 numbering (UK GCE uses 2.4 for national income) — worth verifying the spec mapping across the whole unit.

Repair the block-level wiring: set quizIndices by topic (e.g. block2 → [12,18,21,23], block4 → [5,13,17,9], block5 → [2,22], block6 → [4,7,14,16,19,20], block7 → [6,8,15,24]), point practiceIndices so the 6/10/14-mark questions appear on the matching blocks, add diagramRef 'CPI Basket' to block 3 and 'Types of Unemployment' to block 6, and build an AD/AS diagram (axes: price level / real output) for block 4 so its diagramRef resolves.

Replace the four non-orderable/arbitrary reorders (factor incomes, CPI-vs-RPI differences, ILO criteria, HDI components) with matching/classification exercises, and give fill-ins distractor words plus numeric calculation blanks (real GDP, per-capita, weighted CPI, value added) instead of three-word banks with letter hints.

Close the spec gaps most likely to be examined in WEC12: add an 'Effects of unemployment' subsection, money-supply growth as an inflation cause, 'Limitations of the CPI' (replacing most of RPI-vs-CPI), real-wage unemployment, and a short capital/financial account explainer; swap several UK examples for Asian/Middle-East ones.

Fix the practice set to WEC12 tariffs and marking: Define = 2 marks, drop 'Outline' for 'Explain', convert the 20-mark Evaluate into a 14-mark Discuss (or label it Unit 4 style), and rewrite the 10/14-mark schemes as levels (KAA + Evaluation) rather than point tallies.

Correct the factual slips: Q3 explanation (CPIH does not include mortgage interest; RPI does), 'CPI excludes housing costs', GNI 'citizens' → residents, US CA 'every year since 1982', 2023 RPI–CPI gap and rail-fare claim, the unverified ONS 2024 basket example, and reframe 2021-22 US inflation and the 1930s New Deal claim as mixed/contested.

q3: Explanation states 'CPI does NOT include mortgage interest payments (that's CPIH)'. Wrong: CPIH adds owner-occupiers' housing costs via rental equivalence, not mortgage interest; it is the RPI that includes mortgage interest payments. Also 'substitution bias' (the key) is never taught anywhere in the content, so the pre-test/inline draw can present an untaught concept.

p0: 'Define the term GDP (4 marks)' — in IAL Economics 'Define' items carry 2 marks; the scheme awards marks for the three measurement methods, real vs nominal, and 'most widely used indicator', none of which a define mark scheme credits. Teaches students to pad definitions. This is also the item that surfaces inside the Inflation block in Learn Mode (practiceIndices [0] → sortedPractice[0]).

p3: 'Evaluate... (20 marks)' — WEC12 (Unit 2) papers have no 20-mark essay; the top tariff is 14 ('Discuss') with 12 'Assess'. 20-mark 'Evaluate' is a WEC13/WEC14 format. The scheme is also point-tallied (2+3+2+2+3+2+2+2+2) whereas IAL marks 10+ questions on KAA/Evaluation levels, so the 'model answer' misrepresents how marks are earned.

Inline quiz mapping is broken: block.quizIndices are simply [0],[1],...,[7] and LearnModeTab.jsx:106-108 uses them literally, so block 2 'Uses and Limitations of GDP' shows Q2 (malign deflation), block 4 'Inflation: Causes and Effects' shows Q4 (structural unemployment coal miner), block 5 'Deflation' shows Q5 (cost-push oil), block 6 'Employment and Unemployment' shows Q6 (UK current account), block 7 'Current Account' shows Q7 (LFS vs claimant count). Only blocks 0, 1 and 3 get a topically relevant MCQ.

No diagram ever renders in Learn Mode: block 4 diagramRef 'Demand-Pull and Cost-Push Inflation' matches neither stored diagram title ('CPI Basket of Goods', 'Types of Unemployment') under the substring test at LearnModeTab.jsx:97-104, and blocks 3 and 6 (which those diagrams fit) have diagramRef null. The section has no AD/AS diagram at all, yet demand-pull and cost-push examMatters both instruct students to shift AD/SRAS on a diagram (and never state the axes: price level / real output).

Inline practice mapping: block 4 (Inflation) practiceIndices [0] resolves to sortedPractice[0] = 'Define GDP (4 marks)'; block 6 → 'Outline two types of unemployment' (correct). P1, P2, P3 (the 6/10/20-mark items) never surface in Learn Mode, so students never meet an Assess/Evaluate question in the guided flow.

Every block has exactly 3 sections, so 2-per-step pairing yields [s1,s2] then a lone [s3] step that also carries diagram+quiz+practice+ExplainItBack+takeaway — 16 steps with an uneven 'light, heavy' rhythm. Recall scheduling side-effect (LearnModeTab.jsx:345-359, 397-402): the lone section's recall is shown as 'immediate' at the bottom of its step and again as 'spaced' at the top of the very next step, i.e. 8 recalls (gdp-per-capita, expenditure-method, HDI, measuring-inflation, effects-of-inflation, consequences-of-deflation, causes-and-policies, current-account-surplus) appear twice back-to-back while the middle section's recall appears once and nothing is actually spaced.

recall.shuffled uses only two permutations across all 12 reorders ([2,0,3,1] ×7 and [3,1,0,2] ×5); ReorderRecall.jsx:9 applies them verbatim, so the displayed order is predictable and a student can learn 'swap positions' patterns.

Fill-in word banks are exactly the three answers (FillInRecall.jsx:12), so all 12 fill-ins are 3-item drag-drops with grammatically forced slots; combined with letter-count hints they cannot discriminate understanding.

Terminology drift between layers: content teaches 'demand-side / supply-side deflation', quiz Q2 tests 'malign / benign'; content teaches real GDP via base-year prices, quiz Q1/Q10 test the GDP deflator formula; content never mentions substitution bias but Q3 keys on it. The pre-test draws randomly from all 25, so the gate can be failed on untaught material (consistent with the founder's 'pre-test demotivates' hypothesis).

Sequencing/scope: HDI (Unit 4 development in IAL) sits inside the GDP-limitations block; the Deflation block spends a full subsection on liquidity trap and QE (policy, later units) while the Unemployment block omits the effects/costs of unemployment entirely, so block depth is inverted relative to the spec.

Takeaways match their blocks well and misconceptions are largely genuine student errors (GDP=wealth; disinflation=deflation; deficit always bad; cutting rates always fixes deflation). Two are filler: 'cost-push inflation only comes from oil prices' and 'GDP is useless'.

Difficulty ramp is flat rather than rising: every subsection follows the same template (definition, flow, example, misconception) with no calculation practice until the quiz, so the numeracy the spec demands (index numbers, real growth, per-capita, weighted CPI) is never scaffolded in the notes.
Effects/costs of unemployment on consumers, firms, workers, government and society — entirely absent (block 6 covers measurement, types and policies only).
Growth of the money supply as a cause of inflation — not mentioned (IAL 2.3.1 lists demand-pull, cost-push and money supply growth).
Limitations of the CPI as a measure of inflation (substitution bias, quality change, representative household, basket lag, sampling) — not taught, though tested in Q3 and practice P2.
Effects of inflation on the government and on firms' competitiveness/investment in depth — only savers/borrowers/workers covered; government (fiscal drag, debt erosion, tax revenue) missing.

Real-wage inflexibility (classical) unemployment and the significance of migration and skills for employment — not taught; the 'cutting wages' misconception dismisses the real-wage view rather than explaining it.
Employment rate, economic inactivity rate and the significance of changes in them; underemployment gets a single bullet.
Capital and financial accounts as the counterpart to the current account — mentioned only in passing as the financing source; no structure of the BoP.
Relationship between current account imbalances and other macro objectives, and interconnectedness of economies through trade — not taught.

Value vs volume, index numbers and calculating rates of change/growth from data (a core WEC12 data-response skill) — no worked calculations in the notes; the deflator formula appears only in the quiz.
Weighted-average construction of the CPI with a numerical example — process described in words only.
Unsure: whether IAL 2.3.1 names RPI/CPIH or HDI at all; both are covered here in depth and may be over-coverage of UK-GCE material rather than gaps.

Fix Learn Mode wiring: set diagramRef strings that substring-match the diagram titles ('The AD Curve' for block 2, reuse its shift scenarios for block 3, 'The Multiplier Effect' for block 4) and reassign quizIndices by topic (block 3 -> Q4/Q12/Q16, block 4 -> Q3/Q21/Q24, block 5 -> Q7/Q15) so students stop seeing a multiplier calculation before the multiplier is taught. Also route the 10- and 20-mark practice items into Learn Mode.

Correct the content errors: consumption is NOT the most volatile component (determinants-of-consumption keyIdea); rewrite the 2022-inflation example so BoE rate rises are a shift, not the 'interest rate effect'; fix the car-industry accelerator example (sales fell); replace 'narrowly avoided a recession'; use one currency per example and fix '80p of every extra $1'; align the multiplier formula teaching with Q21.

Replace the 10 non-genuine recalls with application exercises: movement-vs-shift classifier (movements-along-ad), C/I/G/X-M classifier (ad-formula), MPW->k calculation comparison (multiplier-size-determinants), numeric accelerator table (accelerator-definition), scenario-based limitation matcher (limitations); drop leading-letter hints everywhere.

Remove or shrink the duplicated multiplier block (it lives in 2.3.4 national-income with overlapping ids) and use the space for missing 2.3.2 spec bullets: saving vs consumption and MPC/MPS, gross vs net investment, animal spirits and access to credit in the investment body, G over the trade cycle, protectionism and non-price factors for net trade. Cut the accelerator to one subsection.

Rebuild practice to IAL format: Define (2), Explain (4/6), Analyse (8) with a diagram, Assess (10/12), Evaluate (20) with levels-based guidance that sums correctly; add a short data extract and a 'Calculate the multiplier / change in national income' item; strip Marshall-Lerner and J-curve from the WEC12 mark scheme. While there, swap most UK-only examples (and Q8's NHS/JSA) for country-neutral or Asian/Middle-East cases to match the audience.

Components of Aggregate Demand > determinants-of-consumption > keyIdea: States consumption 'is the largest and most volatile component of AD'. Investment is the most volatile component (as the next subsection's keyIdea, the block takeaway 'Investment is the most volatile', and block 5's takeaway all say). Consumption is the largest and the most stable. Direct internal contradiction on a fact IAL examiners test.
content.evidence: audit/snapshots/2026-09-11-post-packet-0__economics__aggregate-demand.json determinants-of-consumption.keyIdea now reads 'most stable component of AD; investment is the most volatile'

content.text: The AD Curve > movements-along-ad > realExample: Claims 2022 UK inflation caused a movement along AD via three effects and lists 'pushed the Bank of England to raise interest rates (interest rate effect)'. The interest-rate effect behind AD's slope is the money-demand mechanism; a central bank raising the policy rate is a discretionary monetary tightening that SHIFTS AD left. The example therefore confuses the exact distinction the subsection exists to teach, and 2022 inflation was a cost-push (SRAS) episode, which the example never mentions.

The Accelerator Effect > accelerator-definition > realExample: Says UK car investment fell in 2017-18 'even though car sales were still at historically high levels' and that a 'slowdown in growth, not an actual decline' triggered it. UK new-car registrations peaked in 2016 (~2.69m) and fell in both 2017 (-5.7%) and 2018 (-6.8%), so demand actually declined. The example contradicts the mechanism it is meant to illustrate.

The Multiplier > multiplier-formula > body para 1 vs quiz Q21: Body defines MPC as 'the proportion of each extra pound ... spent on domestic goods and services' and says k = 1/(1-MPC) is 'equivalent' to 1/MPW. Under that definition it is; but quiz Q21 marks '1/(1-MPC)' WRONG for an open economy with government. The section teaches one thing and tests the opposite.

q21: Distractor [2] '1/(1-MPC)' is presented as wrong, but the section body defines MPC as spending 'on domestic goods and services' and states k = 1/(1-MPC) is 'equivalent' to 1/MPW. Under the section's own teaching two options are correct.

q8: Answer depends on knowing that 'Jobseeker's Allowance' is a UK unemployment benefit and that 'NHS' is a health service. International IAL students (HK, Korea, Pakistan) may not know either; the item then tests UK civics not economics.

p2: 'Analyse ... (10 marks)': in IAL WEC12 'Analyse' is an 8-mark question; 10 and 12 marks are 'Assess'/'Discuss' with evaluation. The scheme awards 4 of 10 marks for Marshall-Lerner and the J-curve, which are Unit 4 (WEC14) content, and lists point-by-point marks where IAL uses levels-based marking for 8+ mark items. No AD diagram is required, which an examiner would expect in KAA.

Inline diagrams never render: block 2 diagramRef 'Aggregate Demand Curve' and block 3 diagramRef 'Shifts in Aggregate Demand' do not substring-match any diagram title ('The AD Curve', 'The Multiplier Effect', 'Circular Flow of Income with AD Components') under the match in components/LearnModeTab.jsx:97-104 (t.includes(ref) || ref.includes(t)). Blocks 4 and 5 have no diagramRef even though 'The Multiplier Effect' exists. Net: 0 of 3 diagrams appear in Learn Mode for this section.

quizIndices are assigned sequentially [0],[1],[2],[3],[4] rather than by topic: block 'Shifts in AD' shows Q2 (multiplier calc, untaught yet), block 'The Accelerator Effect' shows Q4 (AD leftward shift). Only 5 of 25 MCQs are used inline; the two accelerator MCQs (Q7, Q15) are never used.

The 3-subsection 'The Multiplier' block duplicates national-income's 'The Multiplier and National Income' block (national-income uses ids multiplier-concept / multiplier-formula / multiplier-evaluation; this section uses multiplier-definition / multiplier-formula / multiplier-size-determinants -- 'multiplier-formula' is the same id in both files). IAL puts the multiplier under 2.3.4 National income. A student following the unit does the multiplier twice, and if any client-side state is keyed by subsection id it may collide.

Pre-test gate draws 3 random MCQs from a 25-item bank that includes circular-flow (Q9, Q18) and paradox-of-thrift (Q23) items not taught in this section, plus UK-institution items (Q8). A first-time learner can be gated on material the section never teaches -- consistent with the founder's 'pre-test demotivates' hypothesis.

Recall placement side-effect: single-section steps (multiplier-size-determinants, step 6) get their recall shown as 'immediate' at the bottom of that step AND as 'spaced' at the top of the next step, so the not-orderable 'order of logic' reorder is the one widget students meet twice in a row.

Misconception duplication: ad-formula-and-components and determinants-of-gov-spending-net-exports carry the same transfer-payments misconception almost verbatim. Otherwise misconceptions are genuine (MPC<1, 'AD falls' vs 'shifts left', micro substitution reasoning, multiplier != government revenue, accelerator vs multiplier).

Audience fit: 11 of 14 realExamples are UK-centric (house prices, Brexit, furlough, Bank of England, London 2012, OBR, UK car makers, UK 2008, UK 2020) for a HK/Korea/Singapore/Malaysia/Pakistan/Sri Lanka/Middle East cohort; only Apple and Singapore are non-UK. Not wrong for IAL marking, but a mismatch with the product's audience and its own 'international' positioning.

2-per-step pairing is coherent (formula+C; I+G/NX; shape+movements; right+left; concept+formula; size; accel def+cycle; limitations). Block takeaways match their blocks. Difficulty ramp (components -> curve -> shifts -> multiplier -> accelerator) is sensible, but the accelerator gets 3 of 14 subsections -- disproportionate for a topic that is at most an evaluation point, while spec bullets are missing (see ialSpecGaps).
Diagram SVGs hard-code light text (#e8ecf5) with a transparent background: legible only on a dark theme. If the app supports a light theme the axes and labels vanish.

2.3.2(a) relative importance of the components of AD -- only a UK % breakdown; no discussion of why C dominates, why I matters despite its size, or how composition differs (e.g. export-led Singapore/Korea vs consumption-led economies).

2.3.2(b) the distinction between saving and consumption (saving as the residual of disposable income; APC/APS/MPC/MPS) -- not taught in the consumption subsection; MPC only appears later inside the multiplier block.
2.3.2(c) gross vs net investment (depreciation/replacement investment) -- not taught, yet the accelerator block relies on 'net investment' undefined.
2.3.2(c) distinction between investment and saving -- only a one-clause aside ('does not include financial investments like buying shares').

2.3.2(c) influences on investment: 'Keynes and animal spirits' (examMatters only, never in body; tested by Q5), 'demand for exports', 'access to credit' (only as an accelerator limitation), 'influence of government and regulations' -- missing from the investment subsection.
2.3.2(d) government expenditure: G over the trade cycle (automatic stabilisers, counter-cyclical spending) -- one sentence only; fiscal policy link is thin.

2.3.2(e) net trade: effect of domestic real income on imports (income -> M), degree of protectionism, non-price factors (quality, design, reliability) -- missing; only exchange rate, relative inflation and foreign income are covered.
Multiplier ratio/process/MPC-MPS-MPT-MPM/calculation belong to 2.3.4 National income in the IAL spec; present here as a duplicate rather than a gap.
Accelerator: unsure whether the 2018 IAL WEC12 spec requires it explicitly under 2.3.2; treat as extension, not core, and reduce its weight.

Fix the fill-in data shape and renderer mismatch: split every template line to one '___' (changes-in-equilibrium, supply-side-shocks), replace compound tokens like 'rises, rises' with single words, and widen word banks beyond the answer list (add 2-3 distractors) so the 5 trivial fill-ins become real decisions; correct the five hint lengths.

Re-map inline quiz and practice to their blocks: set content[1].quizIndices to LRAS items (5/12/13/21), content[2] to 2/3/24, content[4] to 7/23/18; either stop sorting practice by marks in LearnModeTab.jsx line 80 or reorder practiceIndices so the SRAS block gets the SRAS movement-vs-shift question and the LRAS block gets the LRAS definition/outline; change practice[0] to a 2-mark 'Define' and practice[4] to 'Explain two factors'.

Add a fourth diagram titled to match 'Self-Correcting Mechanism' (negative gap closing via SRAS shift right, positive gap via SRAS left) and rename content[3].diagramRef so blocks 3 and 4 stop rendering without a diagram.

Correct the wrong/contradictory real examples: replace the 2022 UK manufacturers SRAS example, reword 'UK 2019 close to macroeconomic equilibrium' to 'close to full-employment output', fix the 'classical economics had not predicted stagflation' attribution, and use a demand-only case (2008-09 confidence collapse) instead of COVID in demand-side-shocks since applying-adas-to-events later says COVID shifted both curves.

De-duplicate: merge block 3 into block 2 (stagflation and AD-right analysis are taught twice), replace the two generic procedure reorders (ad-as-equilibrium, demand-side-shocks) with concrete causal chains, prune the quiz bank duplicates (Q11=Q1, Q13=Q5, Q14=Q4, Q19=Q8, Q24~Q18) and rewrite Q20 to name the Keynesian model; remove the 'SRAS steepens near capacity' takeaway so SRAS and Keynesian LRAS stay distinct.

content[0] 'Short-Run Aggregate Supply (SRAS)' > sras-shape-and-slope > realExample: Claims UK manufacturers in early 2022 saw margins boosted and expanded production because wages lagged output prices. 2022 was a cost-push squeeze (energy/input costs rose faster than output prices; UK manufacturing PMI fell below 50 from mid-2022 and output declined). The example illustrates the opposite of what happened.

content[2] 'Macroeconomic Equilibrium' > ad-as-equilibrium > realExample: Says the UK in 2019 'was operating close to macroeconomic equilibrium'. An economy is always at AD=AS equilibrium; what is meant is full-employment equilibrium. The section's own misconception two lines later warns that equilibrium is not the same as full employment, so the example teaches the misconception it is correcting.

content[4] 'Policy Conflicts and Trade-Offs' > phillips-curve > realExample: 'The UK in the 1970s experienced stagflation with unemployment and inflation both exceeding 10%.' UK inflation did exceed 10% (peaking ~24% in 1975) but UK unemployment stayed roughly 3-6% through the 1970s and only passed 10% in 1981-82. The stagflation point stands; the number is wrong.

content[3] 'Economies and Diseconomies of Scale' > diseconomies-demergers > realExample: 'eBay demerged Skype in 2009, selling it to Microsoft' is wrong on two counts. (1) Fact: in 2009 eBay sold a ~65-70% stake to an investor group led by Silver Lake; Microsoft bought Skype in 2011 for $8.5bn. (2) Concept: selling a subsidiary to a third party is a divestment/sell-off, not a demerger (a demerger spins the unit off into a separately listed company whose shares go to existing shareholders). This is the section's only demerger example and it teaches the wrong definition.

content[0] 'Business Objectives' > alternative-objectives > realExample: Amazon example muddles the terminology just taught: it says Amazon 'prioritised revenue and market share' then calls this 'sales maximisation' (AR = AC breakeven). Amazon's strategy was long-run growth/revenue maximisation and it was profitable most years after 2003. Also 'reinvesting every pound of revenue' — Amazon is a US firm and you reinvest profit/cash flow, not revenue.

Misconception quality is mixed: types-of-trade-bloc (FTA vs customs union = CET) is the classic real error and is well handled; benefits-costs ('entirely good or entirely bad') and costs-of-mncs ('MNCs are always bad') are the same generic 'be balanced' filler stated twice. The notes[] misconception for the same subsection ('students treat globalisation as entirely new') is a different, better one and is not surfaced in Learn Mode.

Stakeholder framing absent: IAL question stems ask for impact on 'governments', 'producers', 'workers', 'consumers', 'the environment'; the content is organised as benefits vs costs with governments and producers never addressed as stakeholders (diagram 2's 'TNC influence on policy' is the only mention of governments).

Takeaways match their blocks well and the ramp (causes > effects > MNC benefits > MNC costs > bloc types > creation/diversion) is sensible; the 2-per-step pairs are coherent (each pair is a benefit/cost or definition/application couple). This is the section's structural strength.
Characteristics of globalisation (rising trade/GDP, FDI and capital flows, TNC growth, migration, integration of financial markets): not taught in content body; only implied by quiz[0] and diagram 0.

Impact of globalisation on governments (tax competition/'race to the bottom', reduced policy autonomy, tax base erosion) and on producers (access to larger markets, cheaper inputs, global supply chains, competition): spec lists impacts on 'individual countries, governments, producers and consumers, workers and the environment'; governments and producers are not covered as stakeholders.
Growth of TNCs as a factor contributing to globalisation (spec lists TNCs among the causes): TNCs appear only as an effect/actor in block 2; practice[1] asks it but the body never teaches it.
Deindustrialisation in developed economies as an effect (flashcards teach it; content body does not).
'Common market' as the spec term for the third level of integration, and 'economic union' as a level: absent (unsure whether IAL requires economic union explicitly).
Trade creation and trade diversion diagram: examMatters demands it, none provided. Unsure whether the IAL spec requires the diagram, but the concepts sit under spec 4.2 trading blocs, not 4.1.
Brain drain / migration effects on source and host countries: flashcards mention brain drain; content body only mentions migration in a misconception (unsure whether IAL 4.1 or 4.5 expects this).

Add the missing content: a real 'International Competitiveness' section pair (measures: relative ULC and relative export prices; factors; significance) and an 'Effects of Exchange Rate Changes' section (inflation, growth, employment, FDI, competitive devaluation, revaluation/devaluation terminology), plus 'Correcting a current account deficit' in block 1. This makes quiz[5..11] and practice[4] teachable and closes ~8 spec bullets.

Wire the blocks into Learn Mode: add diagramRef ('Balance of Payments Structure' on block 1; 'Exchange Rate Determination' on block 2, J-curve on the new effects block) and quizIndices/practiceIndices so inline quiz and practice match what the step taught.

Add recall widgets from existing flows: reorder on 'Imports exceed exports -> CA deficit -> financed by financial account surplus -> capital inflows' and 'Fed raises rates -> capital attracted -> demand for $ rises -> $ appreciates'; fillin on '|PED_x| + |PED_m| > __' with word bank {exports, imports, 1, 0}.

Fix precision errors: three BoP accounts (not two) in body[0]/keyIdea; 'sum of elasticities < 1' instead of 'inelastic on both sides' in the ML paragraph; replace the Brexit 'textbook J-curve' example with an international one (Sri Lanka 2022 or Turkey 2018-21) worded as 'consistent with'.

Realign practice to IAL conventions: Define 2 marks, Explain 4, Analyse 6, Assess 10/12, Evaluate 14/20; drop 'Outline'; rewrite guidance for the 10- and 20-markers as levels descriptors (KAA + Evaluation) rather than point tallies, and state the diagram expected.

content[1] 'Competitiveness' > marshall-lerner-j-curve > realExample: Claims post-Brexit sterling depreciation produced 'a textbook J-curve' with UK exports 'gradually becoming more competitive' over two years. The UK current account deficit actually narrowed sharply in late 2016 (5.2% of GDP in 2016 to ~3.5% in 2017, driven largely by primary income valuation effects), and the widely discussed empirical finding is the absence of an export volume response (exporters raised sterling prices/margins). Presenting a contested, arguably counter-example as 'textbook' is misleading; a teacher who knows the data will object.
q7: Unit labour costs never appear in content[]. Block 2 is titled 'Competitiveness' but has no competitiveness content. Question and explanation are correct.

p4: 'Outline two measures ... (4 marks)': 'Outline' is not an IAL Economics command word (should be 'Explain'). The topic (measures of competitiveness) is not taught anywhere in content[]. Guidance uses 'real effective exchange rate' where the spec bullet 4.3.3(a) names 'relative export prices' and 'relative unit labour costs'; REER is acceptable but the spec term should appear.

Block 2 is titled 'Competitiveness' (content[1].title) but its two sections are exchange-rate-determination and marshall-lerner-j-curve; there is no section on international competitiveness. Its takeaways do not mention competitiveness either. Retitle to 'Exchange Rate Movements and Their Effects' and add a genuine competitiveness block.

Zero recall widgets in a section with two genuine causal chains already written as flow blocks (balance-of-payments flow: imports exceed exports -> CA deficit -> financed by financial account surplus -> capital inflows; exchange-rate-determination flow: Fed raises rates -> capital attracted -> demand for dollars rises -> dollar appreciates). Both are ideal reorder recalls; ML condition is an ideal fillin ('|PED_ + PED_| > _'). Learn Mode currently offers no retrieval practice at all.

Neither block has a diagramRef (content[0] and content[1] keys are title/sections/takeaway only), although diagrams[] contains five relevant diagrams including the currency-market S/D diagram that examMatters explicitly tells students to draw. If InlineDiagram matches by diagramRef substring, no diagram is ever shown in Learn Mode for this section. Add diagramRef 'Balance of Payments Structure' to block 1 and 'Exchange Rate Determination' (or 'J-Curve') to block 2.

No quizIndices/practiceIndices on either block, so the inline quiz/practice at the end of block 1 (BoP + systems) may draw ML/ULC questions the student has not reached, and the pre-test draws 3 of 12 where 6 test untaught material.

Ordering: exchange-rate-systems (block 1) explains 'if demand for a currency falls, it depreciates automatically' before exchange-rate-determination (block 2) teaches what determines currency demand. Swap so determination precedes systems, or move systems to block 2 after determination.

Step weight: each block is a single 2-section step; block 1 step carries 7 paragraphs + 1 flow + 2 examples + 2 misconceptions before any interaction. With no recalls and no diagram, this is a long passive read, consistent with the product-wide step-0 drop-off.

Misconceptions are genuine student errors (deficit = failing; floating always better; strong currency always good; depreciation auto-fixes deficit). The stronger, more exam-relevant one recorded in common_mistakes (devaluation vs depreciation terminology) is absent from content[] and would be a better misconception for exchange-rate-systems.
extras.chains and notes[] contain competitiveness content (ULC, non-price factors, REER) that never made it into content[]; the Learn Mode path is thinner than the Notes tab for the same section.
4.3.1(a) Components of the BoP: capital account not taught in content (text says two components).
4.3.1(c) Measures to reduce a current account imbalance (expenditure-switching, expenditure-reducing, supply-side policies) - not taught anywhere in content[].
4.3.1(d) Significance of global trade imbalances - not taught in content[] (only quiz[9]).
4.3.2(b) Distinction between appreciation/revaluation and depreciation/devaluation - absent from content[] (only notes/flashcards/quiz[5]).

4.3.2(d) Government intervention in currency markets via foreign currency transactions and interest rates - only implied in the fixed-rate paragraph; no explicit treatment of how a central bank buys/sells reserves or uses rates to defend a rate.
4.3.2(e) Competitive devaluation/depreciation and its consequences - not taught (one line in diagram 4 only).

4.3.2(f) Impact of exchange rate changes on economic growth, employment/unemployment, inflation and FDI flows - not in content[]; only diagram 4 text. Only the current-account impact (ML/J-curve) is taught.
4.3.3(a) Measures of international competitiveness: relative unit labour costs, relative export prices - not taught (tested in quiz[7], quiz[11], practice[4]).
4.3.3(b) Factors influencing international competitiveness (exchange rate, productivity, wage costs, regulation, non-price factors) - not taught in content[] (extras chain only).
4.3.3(c) Significance of international competitiveness: benefits of being competitive, problems of being uncompetitive - not taught.

Note: sub-numbering 4.3.1/4.3.2/4.3.3 is from memory of the 2018 IAL spec; the section id '4.3.3' with the full 4.3 title suggests the app's numbering differs. Bullet content is stated with reasonable confidence; exact lettering unsure.

Replace quiz[5] (Laffer), quiz[6] (occupational immobility), quiz[7] (poverty trap) with on-spec MCQs on mergers/SLC, predatory pricing vs abuse of dominance, and quality standards/performance targets; then add quizIndices, practiceIndices and diagramRef to each block so pre-test and inline items match what the step teaches.

Fix the diagrams: redraw diagrams[0] as a natural-monopoly price-cap diagram (falling LRAC, P=MC vs P=AC caps, Preg not below AC, MC=MR dashed lines at the true intersection); retitle/replace diagrams[2] so privatisation is not shown as a competitive supply shift; add the competitive-market NMW diagram the examMatters demands; draw the kinked post-NMW MCL in diagrams[1].

Add the missing spec content as a new block ('Promoting competition and contestability': deregulation, competitive tendering, promotion of small business; 'Protecting suppliers': monopsony buyers) plus a short 'impact on prices, profit, efficiency, quality, choice' summary table; consider moving the minimum-wage subsection to 3.3.4.
Add recall exercises: fillin on RPI-X (RPI 5%, X 2% → ?%), reorder on merger-control procedure and on the Averch-Johnson causal chain.

De-UK and de-GCE the exam framing: change '25-mark essay' to '20-mark Evaluate'; say 'competition authorities (e.g. CMA, CCCS, KFTC, HK Competition Commission)'; add 2-3 Asia/ME examples (CCCS Grab-Uber 2018 fine, KFTC Google 2021); rewrite practice mark schemes as IAL KAA + Evaluation levels, fix 'Define (4 marks)' and 'Outline'.

content[1] Regulation of Monopoly > privatisation-nationalisation > examMatters: "This is a classic 25-mark essay topic" — 25-mark essays are UK GCE 9EC0 Papers 1/2 Section C. IAL WEC13 essays (Section C) are 20 marks; the highest IAL tariff is 20 ('Evaluate'). Sets wrong exam expectations for the target audience.

diagrams[0] 'Price Regulation of a Monopoly (RPI-X Price Cap)' svg: Geometry contradicts the intended teaching. The regulated price line Preg is at y=170 while the AC curve at Qreg (x=268) is at y≈115 — i.e. AC is ABOVE Preg, so the regulated firm is drawn making a loss, with no mention of this anywhere in checklist/description (the SVG comment even says 'above AC'). Also the MC=MR point is marked at (200,226) but the MC and MR paths actually intersect near (232,228), so the Qm/Pm dashed lines hang in space. The AC is U-shaped, not the falling LRAC of a natural monopoly, which is the case regulators actually price-cap.

diagrams[2] 'Effects of Privatisation and Deregulation': Represents privatisation as a rightward supply shift in a competitive S/D market ('new entry + efficiency gains'). This directly contradicts content[1] > privatisation-nationalisation body[1] ('privatising a natural monopoly simply replaces a public monopoly with a private one') and conflates privatisation with deregulation — exactly the confusion common_mistakes[1] warns against. E1 is also mis-plotted (S1 and D cross near (272,165), not (260,150)).

q5: Not 3.3.5 content (fiscal policy / macro). With the pre-test drawing 3 random MCQs from this bank, students can be tested on it before seeing anything on government intervention in firms. Also appears in inline quiz rotation for a section that never mentions it.
q6: Belongs to 3.3.4 Labour Markets (labour immobility policies), not taught anywhere in this section's content[]. Off-topic for pre-test and inline quiz.
q7: Welfare/tax content (macro / UK-style 'poverty trap'), not in 3.3.5 and not taught in this section. Off-topic for pre-test.

Zero recall exercises (0 reorder, 0 fillin) — the section has no retrieval practice at all between steps; the only checks are 3 inline MCQs. Obvious candidates exist: a fillin on RPI-X arithmetic; a reorder on the merger-control procedure (notification → Phase 1 → SLC test → Phase 2 → remedies/decision), which is a genuine procedural sequence; a reorder on the Averch-Johnson chain (guaranteed return on capital → incentive to over-invest → inflated capital base → productive inefficiency).

No block carries diagramRef / quizIndices / practiceIndices, so LearnModeTab.jsx:117-121 falls back to distributeItems()/matchDiagramsToBlocks(). Result (3 steps, 1 block each): step 0 'Competition Policy' gets quiz[0] (RPI-X arithmetic) + practice 'Define privatisation' — both untaught at that point; step 1 'Regulation of Monopoly' gets practice 'Outline regulatory capture' (taught in block 3); step 2 gets 'Explain two objectives of competition policy' (block 1). All three inline practice items are on the wrong block.

diagrams[2] 'Effects of Privatisation and Deregulation' shares no title word with any block title ('Competition Policy', 'Regulation of Monopoly', 'Government Failure and Minimum Wages'), so matchDiagramsToBlocks() never places it — it is invisible in Learn Mode and only visible on the Diagrams tab.

Pre-test contamination: 3 of 10 MCQs are off-topic (Q5 Laffer, Q6 occupational immobility, Q7 poverty trap); P(at least one off-topic in a 3-question pre-test) = 1 - C(7,3)/C(10,3) ≈ 71%. This is a concrete mechanism behind the founder's 'pre-test demotivates' hypothesis for this section.

Block 3 'Government Failure and Minimum Wages' pairs two unrelated topics into one step. Government failure is Unit 1 content used here as an evaluation lens (fine) and minimum wage is 3.3.4 Labour Markets content; neither is a 3.3.5 bullet. The spec's own 3.3.5 hook for labour is 'protect suppliers and employees: restricting monopsony power of firms', which is only obliquely covered.

The section is not organised around the spec's logic (why intervene → tools: mergers / monopoly control / promoting competition & contestability / protecting suppliers & employees → impacts on prices, profit, efficiency, quality, choice → limits: regulatory capture, asymmetric information). There is no summary of 'impact on prices/profit/efficiency/quality/choice' (spec 3.3.5b), so a student cannot easily answer the standard 'assess the impact of X on consumers/firms' data-response question.

Difficulty ramp is inverted: the most technical material (RPI-X vs rate-of-return, Averch-Johnson, information asymmetry) sits mid-section, while the closing block depends on 3.3.4 prerequisites (MRPL, MCL, ACL) that are assumed rather than recapped.

Takeaways match their blocks and misconceptions are genuine student errors (dominance vs abuse; RPI-X 'prices always fall'; privatisation 'always improves efficiency'; always-draw-competitive-model) — these are good. Flashcards drift off-section (consumer sovereignty, contestable market, deadweight loss, dynamic efficiency are 3.3.3), low priority.
3.3.5a control of monopolies: quality standards and performance targets — not mentioned anywhere in content[] (only price regulation and, via quiz[1], profit regulation).
3.3.5a promote competition and contestability: promotion of small business — absent.
3.3.5a promote competition and contestability: deregulation — appears only in flashcards, common_mistakes[1] and diagrams[2]; never taught in content[].
3.3.5a promote competition and contestability: competitive tendering for government contracts — only in quiz[8]; not taught.

3.3.5a protect suppliers and employees: restricting monopsony power of firms (as buyers, e.g. supermarket-supplier codes) — only the NMW/labour-monopsony angle is covered; the supplier-protection angle is absent.

3.3.5b impact of government intervention on prices, profit, efficiency, quality, choice — no explicit treatment; partially implied in RPI-X and privatisation sections but never framed as the spec's five impacts.
3.3.5c limits to intervention: regulatory capture and asymmetric information — covered (government-failure-intervention; price-cap-regulation body[2]; quiz[9]). No gap.
Unsure: whether IAL 3.3.5 explicitly lists 'nationalisation' under protecting suppliers/employees (I believe it does, and it is covered).

Add two content blocks (or split into separate sections): 'Terms of Trade' (formula, causes, impact, harmful vs beneficial improvement) and 'Trading Blocs' (FTA→CU→common market→monetary union, trade creation vs diversion, conflict with WTO) so that quiz 1,2,3,6,9,11, practice[2] and [4], diagrams[3] and [4] are taught before they are tested; move quiz[8] (Marshall-Lerner) to the exchange-rate section.

Add diagramRef, quizIndices and practiceIndices to both blocks (block 0: diagramRef 'Comparative Advantage', quiz [0,13,5], practice [0]; block 1: diagramRef 'Tariff', quiz [4,10,12,7], practice [1,3]) and add a stopword filter to normalize() in components/learn-mode/utils.js:33 so 'the' can never match a diagram to a block.

Fix diagrams[0] so specialisation shows an unambiguous output gain (partial specialisation by Country A: 30W+35C, B: 40W → 70W+35C) and rewrite the tariff flow result in methods-of-protectionism to 'consumer surplus lost exceeds producer surplus gained plus tariff revenue'.

Add recall widgets: a reorder on the tariff causal chain (tariff → Pw+t → domestic supply expands/demand contracts → imports fall → DWL b+d), a fillin on tariff welfare areas (CS loss = a+b+c+d / PS gain = a / revenue = c / DWL = b+d), and a fillin on the opportunity-cost calculation from the CA table.

Realign practice with IAL conventions: 'Define' 2 marks; 'Explain' 4 marks with the tariff diagram required; replace 'Outline' with 'Explain'; present 10- and 20-mark guidance as levels (KAA + Evaluation) with an explicit diagram and application requirement, and add the Appellate Body paralysis to the WTO section as the key contemporary limitation.

content[1] 'Protectionism and the WTO' > methods-of-protectionism > body[3] flow.result: Result reads 'Net welfare loss — producer gains are smaller than consumer losses plus government revenue'. That inequality is trivially true and is not the welfare argument. The net loss exists because consumer surplus lost (a+b+c+d) exceeds producer surplus gained (a) PLUS government revenue (c). As written it teaches the wrong comparison.

diagrams[0] 'Comparative Advantage: Numerical Example' (Gains from Specialisation panel + checklist[2]): Before: 70 wheat + 30 cars. After full specialisation: 40 wheat + 50 cars. That is +20 cars but -30 wheat, so the panel does NOT show 'total world output increases' as the checklist demands; a student cannot tell whether the world is better off. Full specialisation by the country with absolute advantage in both goods is the classic case where partial specialisation is needed.
content.evidence: audit/snapshots/2026-09-11-post-packet-0__economics__trade-global-economy.json diagrams[0].svg after-figures now '30 wheat + 35 cars' / 'Total: 70W + 35C' / 'Net gain: +5 cars, same wheat'; scenarios[1] relabelled 'Specialisation by comparative advantage' with matching description, so the panel now shows an unambiguous world-output gain

content.text: q1: Correct (109.1) but terms of trade are never taught in content[] — the formula appears only in diagrams[3], flashcards[14] and extras. Because the block has no quizIndices, distributeItems() makes this the ONLY inline MCQ on step 1 (Protectionism + WTO), so the Learn Mode quiz for that step tests an untaught concept.
q2: Correct, but trading-bloc types are not in content[] (only diagrams[4] and flashcards). Can appear in the pre-test before anything is taught.
q3: Correct, but trade creation/diversion is not in content[] (only extras.chains[2], flashcards and common_mistakes[2]).

p4: 'Outline two factors that may cause a deterioration in a country's terms of trade (4 marks)'. 'Outline' is not an IAL Economics command word (Edexcel uses Define/Calculate/Explain/Analyse/Examine/Discuss/Assess/Evaluate). Terms of trade are not taught in content[], yet because practice is sorted by marks this is practice index 1 and therefore the inline practice on step 1 in Learn Mode. Guidance is fine in substance.

Coverage vs assessment mismatch: content[] teaches only comparative advantage, benefits of free trade, protectionism tools/arguments, and the WTO. Terms of trade (quiz 1,6,11; practice 4; diagrams[3]; flashcards[14]; extras.chains[3]), trading blocs / trade creation-diversion (quiz 2,3,9; practice 2; diagrams[4]; flashcards[10-13]; extras.chains[2]; common_mistakes[2]) and Marshall-Lerner (quiz 8) are assessed but never taught. 7/14 MCQs and 2/5 practice questions are untaught.

Only 2 Learn Mode steps (block 0: comparative-advantage + benefits-free-trade; block 1: methods-of-protectionism + the-wto). Each pair is coherent, but the whole spec area is compressed into two screens; the protectionism section crams four tools, four arguments for, four against and a tariff flow into three paragraphs with no explanation of the tariff diagram in the body.

Zero recall objects (meta.reorder 0, meta.fillin 0) so Learn Mode offers no retrieval practice beyond one MCQ per step and the completion screen's recall score is always 0/0. This section has genuinely orderable chains that would suit reorder (tariff imposed → domestic price rises to Pw+t → domestic supply Q1→Q2, demand Q4→Q3 → imports shrink → DWL b+d) and clean fill-ins (CS loss = a+b+c+d, PS gain = a, revenue = c).

Blocks have no diagramRef/quizIndices/practiceIndices, so LearnModeTab.jsx:117-119 uses the legacy fallback. matchDiagramsToBlocks (components/learn-mode/utils.js:31-57) keeps any word longer than 2 chars, so 'the' in 'The Effect of a Tariff (Welfare Analysis)' matches 'The Case for Free Trade' (score 1) and the TARIFF diagram is placed at the end of step 0 before protectionism is taught; 'The Effect of a Quota' then matches 'Protectionism and the WTO' on 'the'. The Comparative Advantage numerical diagram, the ToT diagram and the Trading Blocs diagram never appear in Learn Mode. Fix by adding diagramRef ('Comparative Advantage' / 'Tariff') to the blocks and adding a stopword filter to normalize().

distributeItems (utils.js:9-23) with 14 quiz items and 2 steps gives step 0 → quiz[0] (fine) and step 1 → quiz[1] (ToT calculation, untaught). Practice sorted by marks gives step 0 → practice[0] Define CA (4), step 1 → practice[4] Outline ToT (4). So the protectionism/WTO step's assessment never touches protectionism or the WTO.

PreTest draws 3 random from the 14-item bank (PreTest.jsx:9); with half the bank untaught, the expected pre-test contains ~1.5 questions the student cannot have learned, which reinforces the founder's 'pre-test demotivates' hypothesis for this section specifically.

Takeaways do match their blocks (block 0: CA / static vs dynamic gains / frictions; block 1: protectionism DWL / WTO principles / regionalism). Block 1 takeaway 1 'arguments for it are often abused' is a value judgement stated as a takeaway; better to state the evaluation criterion (temporary, targeted, credible exit).

Misconceptions are real student errors (absolute vs comparative; benefits without limits; tariffs save jobs; WTO enforces free trade), not filler — good. But the comparative-advantage realExample (low labour costs) undercuts the first one.

Difficulty ramp is sensible (concept → gains → intervention → institutions) but ends at the WTO without returning to the numerical/diagrammatic skills the examMatters fields promise ('practise until this is automatic') — there is no worked tariff-diagram walk-through or numerical CA exercise in the flow.

Terms of trade: definition, calculation (index of export prices / index of import prices × 100), factors influencing the ToT, and impact of changes on an economy — entirely absent from content[] (only in diagrams/flashcards/extras/quiz).

Trading blocs: types (free trade area, customs union, common market, monetary union) with examples, and costs and benefits of regional trade agreements including trade creation and trade diversion — absent from content[].

Possible conflicts between regional trade agreements and the WTO — one sentence in the-wto body[2] plus extras.evaluation[2]; not developed (rules of origin, MFN exception under GATT Article XXIV, 'spaghetti bowl').
Patterns of trade: changes in trade patterns between developed and emerging economies, the role of relative exchange rates and trading blocs in shaping patterns — absent.

Absolute advantage: defined only in a flashcard and in passing inside the misconception; no numerical worked example of comparative advantage in the body (only diagrams[0], which is not surfaced in Learn Mode).

Impact of protectionist policies on consumers, producers, governments, living standards and equality — the tariff welfare analysis is only in the diagram; distributional effects (living standards, equality, effect on developing-country exporters) are not covered.
Subsidies to domestic producers: listed as a tool but never analysed (no subsidy diagram, no welfare analysis).

Limitations of the theory of comparative advantage beyond listing assumptions (e.g. increasing costs, dynamic/created comparative advantage, transport costs, externalities) — only in extras.evaluation[0], not in content.
Numbering: unsure of exact sub-numbers, but in WEC14 this material sits under 4.1 (Causes and effects of globalisation), not 4.3.2.

Add body subsections for the untaught spec bullets (income vs wealth inequality; measures and causes of poverty incl. headcount/poverty gap/MPI; inequality between countries; Kuznets/impact of development; capitalism and inequality) so the quiz bank, PreTest and flashcards test what the Learn flow actually teaches.

Fix the relative-poverty/inequality conflation in absolute-relative-poverty (body[1], body[2], flow, realExample 'relative inequality', takeaway[1]) so it agrees with common_mistakes[0]; say inequality rose (Gini) and relative poverty depends on the bottom vs the median.

Rewrite MCQ distractors so the correct option is not the longest (currently 8/10), replace the absurd distractors in quiz[3] and quiz[9] with plausible near-misses, remove the 'within a country' giveaway in quiz[7], and correct quiz[1]'s 'relative poverty exists primarily in developed countries' explanation.

Add recall widgets and diagram hooks: a reorder on the Lorenz→Gini procedure (from notes[1].flow), fillins on the Gini formula/endpoints and the two poverty definitions, and set diagramRef: 'Lorenz' on content[0] and 'Kuznets' on content[1] so InlineDiagram renders.

Update the poverty line to $3.00/day (2021 PPP, June 2025) everywhere ($2.15 '2022 PPP' is mislabelled and superseded), fix the US 91%→70% top-rate claim, and recast practice[2]/[3] guidance as IAL levels-based marking (KAA/Evaluation) while replacing the non-IAL 'Define the difference' and 'Outline' command words.

content[0] 'Types of Poverty' > absolute-relative-poverty > body[0] and keyIdea; diagrams[1] label '(fixed: $2.15/day)'; practice[0].guidance; notes[0]; flashcards[0]: '$2.15 per day (2022 PPP)' is wrong on two counts: the $2.15 line was expressed in 2017 PPP (adopted Sept 2022), and in June 2025 the World Bank raised the international poverty line to $3.00/day at 2021 PPP. As of 2026 the section teaches a superseded figure with a mislabelled base year.

content[0] > absolute-relative-poverty > body[1], body[2], flow.steps[3], realExample ('meaning relative inequality worsened dramatically'), takeaway[1]: Relative poverty is treated as a synonym for inequality. 'Relative inequality' is not a term; a rising Gini driven by the top decile pulling away does not by itself raise relative poverty (share of households below 60% of median), which depends on the median and the bottom of the distribution. The section's own common_mistakes[0] says students must not 'confuse relative poverty with inequality', yet the body does exactly that.

q0: Answer-length cue across the bank: in 8 of 10 MCQs (indices 0,1,2,3,4,6,8,9) the correct option is the longest, usually by a wide margin. A test-wise student can score ~80% without reading the stems. Since the PreTest samples 3 of these, the pre/post-test delta is unreliable.

Zero recall widgets in the section (meta.reorder=0, meta.fillin=0), so the spaced/immediate recall mechanic of LearnModeTab never fires here. Obvious candidates exist in the data already: notes[1].flow ('Rank population by income' → 'Plot cumulative income share' → 'Calculate Gini = A/(A+B)') is a genuine procedure suitable for reorder; the Gini formula and 0/1 endpoints are ideal fillin material.

Neither block carries diagramRef, quizIndices or practiceIndices (content[0] and content[1] have only title/sections/takeaway). InlineDiagram matches by diagramRef substring, so none of the 3 diagrams (including the exam-critical Lorenz curve) appears inside the Learn flow; students only meet it if they visit the Diagrams tab.

Coverage vs testing mismatch: quiz[4] (Kuznets), quiz[7] (between-country causes), quiz[8] (civil war/poverty), quiz[9] (capitalism), practice[3] (globalisation and between-country inequality), practice[4] (effects of poverty) and 8 of 18 flashcards (HDI, wealth tax, minimum wage, equity vs equality, income vs wealth, Kuznets, between-country causes, education) test material absent from content[] body. The PreTest can therefore gate on untaught content, which plausibly feeds the observed step-0 abandonment.

Only 4 subsections for a spec point with ~8 bullets; two steps total. Block 1 (poverty types + Lorenz/Gini) and Block 2 (causes + consequences/redistribution) pair coherently, but the ramp is flat: nothing on measures of poverty (headcount, poverty gap, MPI), income-vs-wealth distinction, or development/Kuznets before the causes block.

Misconceptions: absolute-relative-poverty ('growth automatically reduces all poverty') is a real student error. lorenz-curve-gini ('Gini is a perfect measure') is filler — the real student errors are swapping the axes, reading Gini 0.4 as '40% poor', and drawing the Lorenz curve above the diagonal (common_mistakes[1] already names the axis error and should be promoted into the section). causes-inequality ('caused only by effort or talent') is ideological rather than an exam misconception. consequences-redistribution is really an evaluation point restated as a misconception.

Takeaways match their blocks (Block 1 takeaway[0-3] and Block 2 takeaway[0-3] all trace to body text). Block 2 takeaway[3] name-checks the Laffer curve, which gets one sentence in the body — thin support for a takeaway.

The examMatters fields are good and IAL-consistent (chains of reasoning, define both terms, Gini = A/(A+B)), but three of four end with the same 'this earns the highest marks / top marks' formula, which reads as template output.

content[0] 'Market Failure and the State' > public-goods, merit-goods-redistribution (whole block): Public goods and merit goods are Unit 1 market-failure content (IAL 1.3.3 public goods, 1.3.4 information gaps), not 4.3.5 'Role of the state in the macroeconomy'. Presenting them as the first half of this spec point misdirects revision. Note also Edexcel IAL does not use the term 'merit good' in its spec (it uses information gaps/externalities); the term is fine as vocabulary but should not be framed as the examiner's expected answer.

p0: 'Define the term fiscal policy (4 marks)' does not match IAL command-word conventions: 'Define' is a 2-mark item; 4 marks would be 'Explain'. The guidance then awards marks for expansionary/contractionary/supply-side uses, which are not part of a definition.

Content/assessment mismatch is the defining fault: 0 of 12 MCQs, 4 of 5 practice questions, 5 of 5 diagrams and 4 of 4 extras chains cover 4.3.5 spec material that the four content[] subsections never teach; conversely nothing in quiz/practice tests public goods, merit goods, poverty traps or UBI. Pre-test (3 random MCQs) and post-test therefore measure nothing the section teaches.

Neither block has diagramRef, quizIndices or practiceIndices (content[0] and content[1] keys are only title/sections/takeaway). InlineDiagram cannot substring-match any of the 5 diagrams, so Learn Mode shows none of them; inline quiz/practice selection falls back to arbitrary items unrelated to the block just read.

Zero recall widgets (0 reorder, 0 fillin) in a section whose spec is full of genuine sequences (crowding-out chain, automatic-stabiliser chain, deficit-to-debt accumulation, transfer-pricing mechanism) and definitional contrasts ideal for fillin. Learn Mode is two text-only steps.

Block ordering/difficulty ramp: block 1 is AS-level Unit 1 content (easy, off-spec), block 2 jumps to a compressed whole-course policy overview. There is no build from 'what the state spends and taxes' through 'public finances' to 'policy in a global context', which is the spec's own ramp.

Subsection fiscal-monetary-supply-side compresses three policy tools into three paragraphs with a flow only for monetary tightening; spec 4.3.5(d) needs five tools (adds exchange rate policy, direct controls) plus TNC controls plus policymaker problems. This one subsection would need to become a block.
Takeaways match their blocks, but block 2 takeaway 4 (UBI) elevates an off-spec idea to a headline point.

Misconceptions: public-goods vs publicly-provided (real, good), merit vs public goods (real), fiscal/monetary interchangeable (plausible), 'UBI solves poverty without trade-offs' (filler; not a misconception IAL students hold or are examined on). A real 4.3.5 misconception (deficit = debt; falling deficit = falling debt; indirect taxes are neutral) is only in the quiz explanations.

Sustainability > green-growth > realExample: States the Paris Agreement 'committed 196 countries to limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius'. The Agreement commits parties to hold warming 'well below 2C' and to 'pursue efforts' toward 1.5C. The $100bn/yr climate-finance pledge originated at Copenhagen (2009) and was reaffirmed in the Paris decision text, not established by the Agreement; OECD reports it was first met in 2022, so 'consistently fallen short' is dated.

Sustainability > sustainable-development > examMatters: Claims 'Examiners expect you to ... evaluate the Environmental Kuznets Curve' and green-growth section claims examiners 'want you to evaluate whether green growth is achievable'. I am not aware of EKC, green growth, natural capital or CBDR appearing in WEC14 4.3.6; these examiner expectations look invented. (Sustainability is assessed in Unit 2 as a cost of growth, not here.)

q3: Correct answer (B) is right, but the Lewis model is never mentioned in any of the six Learn subsections; it exists only in diagram 2, flashcards and extras. Students hit this in the pre-test and inline quiz having never been taught it.

Takeaways match their blocks (checked all 12 bullets) - good. But Block 1's takeaway bullet 3 names 'debt' and bullet 4 'multi-dimensional intervention' while the body's flow only shows the savings-gap loop; the debt/commodity/institution links are asserted, not shown.

Notes tab is broader than Learn content (geography, human capital, disease burden, Washington vs post-Washington Consensus) and diagram 4 uses the spec's strategy taxonomy, whereas the Learn text uses a different (SAP/aid) classification. A student switching tabs sees two different maps of the same topic.

Misconceptions: growth-vs-development, barriers-as-checklist, market-led-universal, dismiss-all-intervention and sustainability-means-no-growth are genuine student errors. 'Students present green growth as a cost-free solution' is filler - no IAL question elicits that error. Every misconception uses the identical 'Wrong - ... Instead write:' template, which reads as generated.

Lewis model and Prebisch-Singer are 'taught' only through a diagram (which cannot render inline) and a quiz question. Lewis is a named spec strategy ('industrialisation: the Lewis model') and should have its own subsection, not be relegated to extras.

Sequencing: Block 3 (sustainability) is the least spec-relevant content but is placed last, where completion-rate data shows the fewest students arrive; meanwhile the spec's core 'other strategies' and 'international institutions' bullets have no block at all.
Measures of development beyond HDI: HDI limitations, other indicators (e.g. MPI, IHDI, Gini, % in agriculture, access to clean water) - only Q0 and Q9 touch this; not taught.

Factors influencing growth and development: foreign currency gap; capital flight; demographic factors (population growth, dependency ratio); access to credit and banking; infrastructure (mentioned only as a strategy); education/skills; absence of property rights (one phrase only); non-economic factors (wars, political instability, geography) - taught only in the Notes tab, not in Learn content.
Market-orientated strategies missing: removal of government subsidies; floating exchange rate systems; privatisation (appear in diagram 4 only).
Interventionist strategies missing: development of human capital as a strategy; managed exchange rates; promoting joint ventures with global companies (diagram 4 only).

Other strategies missing entirely: industrialisation via the Lewis model (diagram/quiz only), development of tourism, development of primary industries, Fairtrade schemes, debt relief (flashcards only).
Role of international institutions and NGOs: World Bank, IMF (beyond SAPs), NGOs - absent from Learn content; app's spec map puts IMF/World Bank in 4.3.5 but practice Q4 tests it here.

Unsure: whether sustainability / Environmental Kuznets Curve / green growth is in WEC14 4.3.6 at all - I believe it is not (sustainability of growth is a Unit 2 cost-of-growth point). If confirmed, Block 3 is off-spec and should be cut or demoted.
